documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping governance and economic systems worldwide, yet many countries in the Global South remain dependent on technologies, infrastructures, and governance models produced elsewhere. This dependency reflects deeper patterns of digital colonialism, including data extraction, reliance on foreign cloud systems, and limited capacity to shape AI on local terms. Grounded in African empirical evidence with broader application across the Global South, this paper argues that universities are critical but overlooked institutions in efforts to strengthen AI sovereignty. While governments, firms, and civil society face persistent capability gaps, universities hold mandates that position them to build research capacity, cultivate technical and governance expertise, and coordinate innovation ecosystems. Drawing on political economy and higher education scholarship, the paper develops the Capability–Alignment–Impact (CAI) Framework to explain how universities can contribute to autonomous AI development through three pathways: strengthening foundational knowledge; improving coordination across government, industry, and civil society; and translating expertise into societal impact. The paper concludes by outlining practical implications for policymakers, development agencies, and university leaders seeking to support sovereign AI ecosystems in the Global South.

The article examines the possibilities of using generative artificial intelligence in teaching the discipline “Engineering and Computer Graphics” in the design of robotic models for the processing industry. The feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence models into the design process of robotic systems as a means of developing spatial thinking, graphic competence, design skills, and digital skills of agricultural university students is substantiated. It is established that modern generative systems (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Claude, DALL·E, etc.) support all stages of educational design, from developing technical specifications and generating product concepts to creating drawings and three-dimensional models, visualizing designs, preparing technical documentation, and analyzing possible design solutions. A methodology for using generative artificial intelligence in the educational project “Design of a Robotic Manipulator” is proposed. The methodology is based on the principles of project-based learning, STEM education, the competency-based approach, and the use of CAD systems. A structural model for integrating generative artificial intelligence into the process of graphic training has been developed. It includes the stages of problem formulation, concept generation, sketch creation, three-dimensional modeling, preparation of design documentation, and expert evaluation of the finished product. It is demonstrated that the use of generative AI contributes to increasing students’ motivation, developing engineering thinking, fostering digital literacy, and reducing the time required for routine operations in the design of robotic models.

documents.abstract: The article examines main aspects of artificial intelligence use in master's degree teaching of Linguistics and Pedagogical Education spheres. Artificial intelligence is currently being actively integrated into the educational process, transforming traditional formats into a more dynamic one: it quickly analyzes information, adapts materials on demand, systematizes and structures information, and personalizes educational content. In this article, the authors emphasize the competent training of future specialists/qualified personnel who will possess in-depth knowledge of the theory and methodology of teaching foreign languages, as well as skills in using innovative technological advances in professional teaching, and will be in demand in the future labor market. Based on the conducted research, the essence of using AI tools in the educational and linguistic environment is revealed, allowing for increased individualization and interactivity in the foreign language learning process. The modern education system is currently undergoing an active digital transformation, driven by the rapid development of information technology and artificial intelligence (AI). It was concluded that artificial intelligence can offer enormous potential for improving the quality of education, reducing the time and effort required by teachers, and facilitating the independent work of master's students. The obtained results allowed us to expand the scientific understanding of the use of AI in educational process and identify solutions for its application by higher education teachers in practical classes. The study materials will be useful for education and philology researchers and teachers improving the educational process.

Mapping an atomic structure to a compact set of geometric descriptors is an essential step in any machine-learning application to atomic-scale modeling. A powerful and widely used approach can be understood as a discretization of the histogram of pair distances, triangles, etc., which results in a hierarchy of symmetry-invariant atom-centered descriptors. Unfortunately, the lower rungs on this hierarchy (two, three, four-body clusters) were found to be incomplete, with symmetry-unrelated pairs of structures having exactly the same descriptors. However, all the "degeneracies" reported so far are resolved by considering larger clusters of neighbors to build the descriptors. We report examples of 3D structures that are indistinguishable even if one considers clusters of up to seven neighbors, and to arbitrary order when considering a practical level of discretization of the descriptors, discovered with the assistance of large language models. The key ingredients in their construction can be traced to results that have been known for decades in different communities: the model was able to find the references and recognize their significance for the problem at hand. We believe that this experiment exposes an extremely fruitful usage pattern for Artificial Intelligence in science: translating results between different communities and application domains, accelerating the process by which serendipitous discoveries in a field become breakthroughs in another.

Occupant-centric building operation requires models that can not only predict thermal sensation, but also justify predictions through auditable reasoning. Traditional mechanistic models, such as Fanger’s predicted mean vote (PMV), often show limited field accuracy, whereas advanced machine learning models can improve prediction but typically remain opaque to facility managers and building operators. This study proposes a verifier-guided knowledge distillation framework for auditable thermal comfort reasoning using a lightweight LLaMA-3.2-3B student model. The framework consists of three sequential stages: (1) knowledge distillation from a teacher model, GPT-4o, to transfer domain-specific explanatory patterns; (2) supervised fine-tuning with ground-truth anchoring and a TSV-weighted loss to improve thermal sensation vote (TSV) prediction while limiting teacher-error propagation; and (3) verifier-guided direct preference optimization using an automated claim-consistency verifier. The verifier extracts factor-direction claims from generated explanations, such as high air temperature or low air speed, and checks them against comfort-centered percentile thresholds derived from the ASHRAE Global Thermal Comfort Database II. On the held-out test split, the final model achieved 42.7 % exact TSV accuracy and 79.9 % ±1 accuracy, comparable to standard tabular baselines on the same split. More importantly, the verifier-guided alignment stage reduced the any-incorrect-claim rate from 52.3 % to 16.5 % and improved linked claim accuracy to 78.3 %. Robustness tests showed reasonable directional consistency under perturbation without strong dependence on PMV or SET proxies. At the hot and cold tails, 81 % of explanations named an HVAC-controllable factor, so compact language models can pair thermal comfort predictions with verifiable, operator-actionable explanations for building operation.

Bicycles are one of the most power-efficient ( di Prampero et al. , 1979 ) and environmentally sustainable methods of human mobility ( Massink et al. , 2011 ). To ensure a comfortable ride, they rely upon a range of mechanical components, pneumatic tyres, and adequate surface conditions. Bicycle dynamics are difficult to model due to the intricate interaction of multiple rigid bodies, with the rider&s;s mass, which constitutes the majority of the system, significantly contributing to its behaviour ( Meijaard et al. , 2007 ). Vibration can be dealt with in a number of ways, including shock absorbers and material damping in a bid to achieve a comfortable and efficient experience for the rider. The topic of vibration measurement has received attention in relation to bicycle component performance, human–machine interaction, and the transmission of the surface condition to the rider. This chapter aims to provide an overview of the science of bicycle-related vibration measurement along with sufficient literature review and technical guidance to facilitate the measurement of vibration for mechanical engineering or human factors research.

Facial video provides behavioural measurements and camera-derived physiological signals that may complement mental health assessment. Their clinical interpretation, however, depends on the acquisition conditions, reference labels, population, and evaluation protocol. This critical narrative review examines facial analysis for mental health screening and symptom estimation, distinguishing depression, anxiety symptoms, experimentally elicited stress, and other condition-specific assessment tasks. We distinguish questionnaire-defined screening labels, symptom severity, experimentally elicited affect or stress, and clinician-established diagnoses. We review image acquisition and preprocessing, facial action units and movement, remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), temporal architectures, and multimodal fusion. Dataset resources are separated by evidential purpose, and representative quantitative results are accompanied by their targets, modalities, and validation conditions rather than presented as a cross-study ranking. The synthesis identifies three recurring limitations: few independent participants despite many video frames, limited validation across populations and recording domains, and a gap between benchmark prediction and clinical utility. Accurate average pulse rate estimation does not establish reliable beat-to-beat variability or disorder-specific validity. We therefore emphasise participant-level evaluation, probability calibration, prevalence-dependent predictive values, acquisition quality, consent, and prospective clinical assessment. Foundation models and longitudinal monitoring remain research directions whose incremental value must be established against appropriate baselines. Current evidence supports investigation of complementary screening and decision support tools, rather than autonomous diagnosis or a demonstrated ability to predict disease onset.

Abstract The arrival of publicly-accessible generative-AI tools, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, has significantly disrupted standard practice in education, research, and publishing. Academic publishers and journals, in particular, have responded by adopting policies which reflect both how they perceive the problems that generative-AI tools pose, and what kinds of solutions address these issues while remaining consistent with key scholarly values: integrity, transparency, and the primacy of human authorship. This article surveys the current state of generative-AI in academic publishing—including relevant policies at the publisher and journal-level—in anticipation of the JBI’s forthcoming policies concerning generative-AI disclosure in manuscript submission and peer-review. Mirroring the emerging policy consensus concerning generative-AI use in academic publishing, this paper proposes that ‘AI-disclosure statements’ constitute an adaptive ‘middle path’ between prohibition and unrestricted permissiveness. Beyond this, though, we argue that AI-disclosure statements are valuable for their potential to codify desirable norms governing generative-AI use in publishing, and so to subtly influence the underlying ‘academic form of life’ for the better. We conclude by discussing one possible outcome of this influence, suggesting that it may represent a solution to problems raised by recent criticism of AI-disclosure statements.

Abstract Recent research shows that anthropomorphizing of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies, such as virtual assistants or chatbots, affects users’ trust. This paper explores what an AI technology should look like at the interface to facilitate appropriate trust. It proposes an integrated framework based on related work, including Lee and See’s (2004) trust in automation model, Mollerup’s (2019) pretense design, as well as Clark and Fischer’s (2023) notion of depictions, for analysis and design of appearances of AI applications that pretend to be something different. Following the proposed framework, cases of AI applications are analyzed. They span a spectrum of appearances, from humans with open or specifc identities, through talking animals, to plants. Analyses suggest that appearances of AI applications should faithfully reflect the actual ability, characteristics, and design intent, in order to facilitate users’ trustworthiness assessments of the applications. Lastly, design implications and future research are discussed.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly present in children’s lives, yet exposure does not necessarily lead to an accurate understanding of how AI works. This study examined whether a LEGO-based integrated STEM intervention could improve third-grade students’ AI literacy and computational thinking, particularly their ability to distinguish machine learning from rule-based automation and reason about training data, model error, and technology choice. An embedded mixed-methods, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest control-group design was conducted with 93 students from four intact classrooms. The experimental group (n = 46) completed eight weeks of authentic design problems, while the control group (n = 47) continued regular Life Studies instruction. After controlling for pretest scores, the experimental group significantly outperformed the control group in AI literacy, F(1, 90) = 152.51, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.629, and computational thinking, F(1, 90) = 22.18, p < .001, partial η2 = 0.198. Qualitative evidence showed a shift from viewing AI through robots and automatic actions toward reasoning about learning from examples, data diversity, limitations, human oversight, accessibility, and problem–technology fit. Integrated STEM instruction can foster critical AI literacy by making AI mechanisms visible and inviting students to judge whether AI is needed at all.

The Difference Between Being Remembered and Being Understood There is something profoundly human about the experience of being remembered. A familiar voice, a shared reference, or an acknowledgment of something that mattered in an earlier encounter can transform an otherwise ordinary exchange into one characterized by continuity. We recognize that our history has not disappeared simply because the previous conversation ended. In human relationships, this continuity can become a foundation for trust, familiarity, and the gradual development of shared understanding. Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of participating in certain computational dimensions of this process. Persistent memory enables systems to retrieve earlier conversations, recognize recurring preferences, resume unfinished activities, and adapt their responses to the histories of individuals with whom they interact. As these capacities converge with multimodal perception and embodied robotics, artificial agents may also begin to initiate interactions based on what they believe they know about a person. Yet this development introduces a distinction that deserves greater attention: remembering someone accurately is not necessarily the same as understanding how to respond to them appropriately. Consider a companion robot that recognizes an individual returning home after a difficult day. Through previous encounters, the system may have learned that the person sometimes appreciates conversation or reassurance during stressful circumstances. Its memory could be accurate, its recognition successful, and its conversational response entirely consistent with earlier preferences. Nevertheless, initiating a supportive exchange may be precisely the wrong action if the person presently needs solitude, concentration, or the freedom to remain unobserved.

documents.abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa carries a disproportionate share of the global burden of antimicrobial resistance. Western sub-Saharan Africa has the highest death rate attributable to resistance of any world region, at 27.3 per 100,000. [1] Yet the region has some of the thinnest data and diagnostic infrastructure on which modern stewardship depends. [2] This is the setting into which artificial intelligence is now being introduced. Machine learning tools are being developed to predict resistance, guide empirical therapy, and flag inappropriate prescriptions, promising data-driven stewardship in exactly the settings where the need is greatest. [3] The prevailing question about these tools is whether they improve stewardship. That question asks for an average effect. Averaged across hospitals with varying infrastructure, artificial intelligence's effect on stewardship may look small, and be misread as evidence that it is not ready for African hospitals. More likely, its effectiveness depends on data and infrastructure that some hospitals have and others do not, so judging it by an average becomes a question of equity. This calls for a different question. The success of AI-supported stewardship in sub-Saharan Africa will not be settled at the level of the technology; it will turn on particular combinations of enabling conditions. It should therefore be studied configurationally, asking under what combinations of infrastructural, epidemiological, and human conditions it works, rather than evaluating it for an average effect.An artificial intelligence tool is not a single intervention, but a bundle of preconditions that must hold together for the tool to help. These preconditions span three dimensions, and each is unevenly met across sub-Saharan Africa. The author received no specific funding for this work.

documents.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are rapidly transforming how people create and experience sexual content, including the emergence of AI-generated pornography (AI-porn). Yet little is known about who is engaging with this evolving medium. This study presents findings from a cross-sectional survey (data collected in 2025) of 367 heterosexual Australian adults (age range = 19–87 years, M = 39.07, SD = 13.43; 52.5% men, 44.8% women [and 2.2% non-binary, excluded from inferential analyses due to small cell sizes]) examining demographic, ideological, and relational correlates of AI-porn familiarity and use. Overall, 26.0% of participants reported having used AI-porn and were moderately familiar with it. Regression analyses showed that men and younger participants were significantly more likely to be familiar with and to have used AI-porn. Ideological factors (religiosity, political orientation) and relational factors (relationship status, relationship and sexual satisfaction) were not associated with use. These findings suggest that engagement with AI-porn is emerging most prominently among digitally curious younger men, yet appears ideologically broad and not linked (in this data set) to relationship dissatisfaction. As AI tools enable new forms of personalized, creative sexual expression, understanding who is exploring these technologies can help researchers and clinicians track evolving norms around intimacy, fantasy, and sexual media in the digital age.

Artificial intelligence is moving from isolated experimentation into everyday enterprise workflows, knowledge repositories, business applications, and increasingly agentic systems. This paper argues that secure AI adoption should be treated as an enterprise governance and business-risk issue rather than as a narrowly scoped information-technology project. It proposes the Five Pillars of Secure AI Adoption, an author-developed framework comprising governance and accountability, data protection, identity and least privilege, AI-specific security controls, and monitoring and incident response. The framework provides an executive-oriented operating model informed by established resources, including the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, the NIST Generative AI Profile, ISO/IEC 42001, and OWASP guidance for large-language-model and generative-AI application security. The paper concludes that security should enable responsible AI innovation through explicit ownership, controlled access, bounded agency, AI-aware safeguards, and observable operations.

documents.abstract: BackgroundPhysiotherapy technicians are frequently exposed to heavy workloads and high patient volumes, which can lead to physical and emotional strain. Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) and burnout are common among healthcare workers and may negatively impact job satisfaction and overall occupational health. Data specifically addressing physiotherapy technicians, however, remain limited.ObjectiveTo examine the prevalence of WMSDs, burnout, and job satisfaction among physiotherapy technicians working in public and private hospitals.MethodsThis observational study was conducted between April 2025 and March 2026. A total of 122 physiotherapy technicians employed in public and private hospitals in Istanbul were included. Demographic data were recorded. The Extended Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire assessed musculoskeletal disorders, the Maslach Burnout Inventory evaluated burnout, and the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire measured job satisfaction. Differences between groups and correlations among the study variables were analyzed.ResultsMusculoskeletal pain at any point in life was reported by 91.8% of participants, most commonly in the neck, lower back, and upper back. Musculoskeletal disorder scores were negatively correlated with job satisfaction and positively correlated with emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, and total burnout scores. Strong negative correlations were observed between job satisfaction and burnout subdimensions. Technicians in private hospitals had lower job satisfaction and higher emotional exhaustion and depersonalization scores than those in public hospitals.ConclusionsWMSDs are highly prevalent among physiotherapy technicians and are significantly associated with increased burnout and reduced job satisfaction. Implementing workplace ergonomic interventions, improving working conditions, and providing ergonomics training are essential to protect employee health and enhance work performance.

The increasing use of computers in the workplace has made ergonomics something that organizations need to pay attention to. This is especially true in the information technology field, where workers often sit at their desks for hours and deal with a lot of mental and technical stress. Some earlier studies have looked at how work setups affect employee being and quality of work life.. There is still not enough focus on how psychological well-being acts as a link between ergonomic practices and quality of the job life for IT laborers. Further study is required to comprehend this link. The current study looks at the connection, between workplace practices and quality of professional life and checks if mental health and wellbeing is the factor that connects them. A study was done using a method that looks at formation from a facts group of people at one moment in time. A special questionnaire was given to 200 IT workers. The study looked at how people feel at work how their jobs affect their mental health and how good their work life is. Each of these areas was measured using a scale that has five options. The researchers used methods to understand the data. They checked how reliable the questions were. They also looked at how the different factors are connected. They found that the questions about each topic were reliable. They found that the way the workplace is set up for employees has an effect, on how they feel and how good their work life is. WP-AI-8.4 develops a Capability-Safety-Responsibility Alignment Framework for governing the release of advanced AI systems into society. The paper begins from a structural distinction: capability advancement and social release are not the same governance question. Scientific and engineering progress determines what AI can do; governance must separately determine what capabilities may enter society, under what safety conditions, through whose authority, and with what responsibility attached. The framework argues that capability growth does not itself create a right to release. Social release should be justified by necessity, demonstrated governability, appropriate safety conditions, and an identifiable responsibility structure. Release is treated as a graduated and reversible process rather than a one-time product event, and material capability expansion after deployment is defined as a form of capability creep that should trigger renewed review. The paper further proposes that release boundaries should be defined by real-world exposure rather than by labels such as testing, evaluation, or experimentation. Where high-risk systems require realistic testing, the paper introduces the concept of a high-fidelity isolated “Shadow World” in which relevant real-world complexity can be reproduced without exposing the open world to uncontrolled experimental consequences. Drawing on the governance logic used in high-consequence technologies such as nuclear systems, the framework emphasizes staged safety review, staged authorization, cumulative responsibility, and legal accountability across the development, approval, deployment, configuration, and operational chain. It also introduces a non-propagation responsibility: organizations deploying generative AI should be responsible for ensuring that failures within their own controlled environment do not propagate into external networks, other institutions, unrelated users, or society. WP-AI-8.4 builds on the preceding papers in the WP-AI-8 series. WP-AI-8.1 established the engineering circuit-breaker principle; WP-AI-8.2 examined responsibility escape; WP-AI-8.3 connected capability control and human responsibility through a dual-track governance framework. WP-AI-8.4 extends this architecture to the release boundary itself, asking when and under what conditions AI capability may move from controlled development into social deployment.

documents.abstract: The article provides a comprehensive examination of the evolution of theoretical approaches to innovation management and identifies the major directions in the transformation of its conceptual foundations under the influence of economic, technological, organizational, and societal changes. The relevance of the study is determined by the fact that, in an increasingly dynamic competitive environment, characterized by digital transformation, the spread of open innovation, the development of innovation ecosystems, platform-based business models, and artificial intelligence, traditional approaches to managing innovation activities require substantial reconsideration. The evolution of academic thought demonstrates a gradual shift from viewing innovation primarily as the outcome of a firm's internal research and technological development activities toward understanding it as a complex, systemic process of creating, disseminating, and commercializing new knowledge, technologies, products, services, processes, and business models involving multiple actors within an innovation ecosystem. he purpose of the study is to systematize and generalize the main stages in the evolution of innovation management theories, identify the underlying logic of the transformation of relevant theoretical paradigms, and substantiate the specific features of the contemporary stage of innovation management development, which is characterized by openness, ecosystem-based interaction, digitalization, the development of dynamic capabilities, and the use of artificial intelligence. The methodological foundation of the study comprises a combination of general scientific and specialized research methods. The historical and logical method was used to identify the sequence of formation and transformation of innovation management theories; the methods of analysis and synthesis were applied to systematize the principles of contemporary theoretical concepts; the comparative method was used to identify the common and distinctive characteristics of the principal paradigms; the systems approach was employed to examine the interrelationships between innovation strategy, resources, organizational capabilities, innovation processes, external partners, and ecosystems; and the generalization method was used to develop an integrated understanding of the contemporary innovation management model. The theoretical and informational basis of the study comprises recent academic works by international and Ukrainian scholars addressing innovation management, open innovation, dynamic capabilities, innovation ecosystems, digital technologies, business model innovation, and artificial intelligence. The scientific novelty of the study lies in systematizing the evolution of innovation management theories as a successive transition from resource- and technology-based and linear models to process-based, capability-based, open, ecosystem, digital, and human–AI hybrid paradigms. These concepts are interpreted not as mutually exclusive approaches, but as interconnected stages in the expansion of the subject matter and scope of innovation management. The study substantiates that the contemporary transformation of innovation management is manifested in a shift from managing individual innovation projects toward developing and enhancing a firm's innovation capabilities, managing knowledge and partnership networks, and orchestrating innovation ecosystems. It is demonstrated that digitalization and artificial intelligence constitute a qualitatively new stage in the development of innovation management theory, in which innovation processes increasingly take the form of human–machine hybrid systems. The study identifies the principal patterns underlying the development of theoretical approaches to innovation management. It is established that the initial focus on technological resources, research and development has gradually been complemented by process-based approaches, the concept of dynamic organizational capabilities, open innovation, innovation ecosystems, and digital transformation. The findings demonstrate that contemporary innovation management encompasses not only the creation of new products and technologies but also the management of knowledge, organizational change, business models, partnership networks, digital data, and intelligent technologies. The principal stages of theoretical evolution are systematized according to the object of management, sources of innovation, the role of the firm, and mechanisms of value creation. The study substantiates the need to integrate process-based, strategic, resource-based, network, ecosystem, and digital approaches into a contemporary innovation management model. It is established that the future development of innovation management theory is associated with the formation of responsible innovation management models, the integration of human and artificial intelligence, the development of digital innovation ecosystems, and the increasing importance of firms' dynamic capabilities. The findings can be used to further develop the theoretical and methodological foundations of innovation management, formulate innovation strategies, and design practical mechanisms for strengthening firms' innovation capabilities.

The article examines the theoretical and practical principles of the functioning of e-commerce enterprises in service markets under the conditions of digital transformation of the economy. The essence of service e-commerce is defined, its specific features are identified, and the main types of services that can act as independent objects of electronic purchase and sale are systematized. Particular attention is paid to the characteristics that distinguish e-commerce in services from electronic trade in tangible goods, including the intangibility of services, the simultaneity of production and consumption, the impossibility of storing unused capacity, personalization, the global nature of digital interaction, and the critical role of digital platforms. The study systematizes the main risks faced by e-commerce enterprises, including cyber, technological, legal, reputational, financial, competitive, marketing, and operational risks. The economic specificity of service e-commerce is associated with the combination of service intangibility, the decisive role of digital platforms as an environment for interaction, and a high level of information asymmetry between sellers and consumers. The importance of mechanisms for preliminary verification of service providers, standardization of service quality criteria and contractual conditions, payment and personal data protection, documentation of service delivery, guarantees, and alternative dispute resolution is substantiated. The study also emphasizes the importance of customer trust, transparency of digital transactions, and the availability of reliable feedback mechanisms, which directly affect consumer decision-making and the long-term sustainability of service providers in digital markets. It is concluded that the efficiency and competitiveness of e-commerce enterprises depend on their digital maturity, management quality, adaptability, and ability to implement innovative technologies. Further development is associated with artificial intelligence, business process automation, and the creation of integrated digital ecosystems.

The article substantiates the role of innovative management tools as a lever for the development of product IT companies under conditions of environmental turbulence, shortening digital product life cycles and intensifying global competition for users and for qualified specialists. It is shown that a product IT company constitutes a specific object of management, characterised by a high share of intangible assets, the transfer of market demand risk to the company itself, the network nature of value and a critical dependence of results on the quality of managerial decisions rather than on the volume of resources involved. Consequently, the traditional lever of growth, namely the accumulation of resources, demonstrates sharply diminishing returns, whereas the returns on the managerial lever increase. The paper clarifies the content of the concept of an innovative management tool, defined as a formalised and reproducible means of influencing the management system that changes the mechanism of decision-making, resource allocation or coordination and provides a measurable increase in organisational adaptability. A five-element classification is developed according to functional purpose, covering tools of strategic goal-setting and alignment, organisational and process tools, product discovery tools, analytical and measurement tools, and human-centred tools including digital and artificial intelligence solutions. A lever model is proposed that explains the conversion of a managerial innovation into growth of company value through four transmission links: shortening of the feedback loop, an increase in the share of validated decisions, growth of value-stream throughput and retention of key competence. A methodological approach to evaluating implementation performance is grounded on an integral index that aggregates five groups of partial indicators using minimax normalisation and expert weighting, accompanied by an interpretation scale distinguishing imitative, fragmentary and systemic implementation. The correspondence between tools and the stages of a company life cycle is established, and barriers to implementation in the Ukrainian context are identified.

The article substantiates the conceptual foundations for forming a digital security ecosystem in the tourism and hospitality industry. It is established that the digital transformation of tourism and hospitality enterprises and the spread of online booking platforms, mobile services, artificial intelligence, geographic information systems, the Internet of Things and cloud technologies simultaneously expand safety management capabilities and create new cyber, information, operational and reputational risks. The concept of a «digital security ecosystem in the tourism and hospitality industry» is clarified as an integrated human-centred environment for interaction among tourists, enterprises, digital platforms, public authorities, insurance and financial institutions, and emergency services, within which continuous data exchange, monitoring, forecasting, prevention, localisation and risk minimisation are ensured at all stages of the tourist journey. The main groups of threats are systematised, and the stakeholder, information, technological, functional and institutional components of the ecosystem are identified. The author’s Digital Security Ecosystem for Tourism and Hospitality (DSETH-model) is proposed, combining digital identification, data integration, risk monitoring, predictive analytics, communication, response and recovery. The principles of its functioning are substantiated: integration, interoperability, prevention, continuity, adaptability, cyber resilience, confidentiality, reliability, inclusiveness and accountability. The stages of practical ecosystem implementation and a set of indicators for assessing its effectiveness are determined. Particular attention is paid to the integration of digital technologies into a unified security environment capable of supporting proactive risk management and improving coordination among all stakeholders. The proposed conceptual framework may serve as a methodological basis for developing digital security strategies and implementing innovative management solutions in the tourism and hospitality industry. It is proved that applying an ecosystem approach will help reduce threat response time, increase consumer trust, strengthen the resilience of enterprises and tourism destinations, improve service quality and enhance the competitiveness of the tourism and hospitality industry.

Artificial intelligence adoption is expanding across the European Union, while national averages conceal substantial firm-size differences. Absolute and relative gaps describe different dimensions of this diffusion. The paper examines cross-country and firm-size inequality in AI adoption across all 27 EU Member States and distinguishes absolute distance from proportional disadvantage. The empirical base is Eurostat’s 2026 statistical report with 2025 country-by-size adoption rates. The absolute gap is the large-enterprise rate minus the small-enterprise rate; the normalised gap divides this difference by their sum. Spearman rank correlations are primary and Pearson coefficients supplementary. Because the official all-enterprise rate is size-weighted and correlates almost perfectly with small-enterprise adoption, relative-gap inference relies mainly on an equal-weight measure averaging small, medium and large enterprises. A medium-enterprise-only correlation provides a check independent of the normalised-gap formula. Coefficients of variation use the population standard deviation for the complete set of 27 Member States. AI was used by 17.0% of small and 55.0% of large EU enterprises. Small-enterprise adoption ranged from 4.1% to 37.5% across countries (CV=0.515), compared with 20.8% to 79.4% among large enterprises (CV=0.274). The national adoption rate is moderately positively associated with the absolute gap (Spearman ρ=0.477, p=0.012). The equal-weight measure is strongly negatively associated with the normalised gap (ρ=−0.816, p<0.001), and the medium-enterprise check is even stronger (ρ=−0.846, p<0.001). Among non-users, only 12.7% of small enterprises had considered AI adoption, compared with 36.5% of large enterprises; reported implementation barriers differed much less across size classes. Cross-country relative dispersion is substantially greater among small enterprises. A higher size-standardised adoption level can coexist with a sizeable absolute large-small distance while being associated with a markedly smaller proportional disadvantage of small firms. The results are cross-sectional associations based on published Eurostat point estimates and do not establish causality.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The article examines the transformation of the advertising services market within the e-business ecosystem, emphasizing the contradictory influence of global economic fragmentation and sustainable development imperatives. It is shown that the digitalization of advertising, the platformization of e-business, the diffusion of algorithmic technologies and artificial intelligence are reshaping interactions among advertisers, digital platforms and e-consumers and changing the mechanisms of creating, distributing and evaluating advertising value. The study argues that the technological globalization of advertising increasingly coexists with institutional, regulatory, technological and data fragmentation of the digital environment. This combination creates a fundamentally new configuration of the global advertising market, in which the growing technological interconnectedness of market participants is accompanied by increasing differentiation of regulatory regimes, digital ecosystems and conditions for accessing consumer data. Particular attention is paid to the growing concentration of platforms and investment resources, the regional differentiation of data governance rules, and the increasing role of AI-driven advertising, retail media and programmatic technologies. It is emphasized that these processes strengthen the role of data, algorithms and digital infrastructure as strategic resources of advertising activities and simultaneously increase the dependence of e-business entities on technological platforms and their ecosystems. Sustainable development is considered not only as a communication agenda but as a criterion for organizing advertising production and delivery, including responsible data use, carbon efficiency, algorithmic transparency, inclusiveness and consumer trust. In this context, the transformation of advertising efficiency criteria is substantiated, as economic performance is increasingly complemented by environmental, technological, ethical and social dimensions. The article develops an original transformation matrix and a conceptual model linking global fragmentation, digital platforms, data, algorithms, sustainable development and the transformation of e-business. The proposed approach makes it possible to interpret the contemporary advertising services market as a complex platform-algorithmic ecosystem whose development is determined by the interaction of technological, economic, institutional, environmental and behavioral factors. Four scenarios for the advertising services market up to 2030 are outlined: inertial, fragmentation-based, platform-algorithmic and sustainable-adaptive. The sustainable-adaptive scenario is identified as the most balanced trajectory for the long-term development of the advertising services market and e-business ecosystem. It is concluded that the advertising market is moving from an economy of advertising reach toward an economy of algorithmically managed, adaptive and responsible interaction with consumers, in which technological efficiency, strategic adaptability and responsible sustainability become interconnected determinants of long-term competitiveness.

This document, S15. Observations on the Fundamentals of Aesthetic Cognition, belongs to the Five Ways · One Law knowledge repository, categorized under observational records (ShiBu). It is a collection of personal phenomenological observations rather than a formal deductive theory or conclusive research paper. No definitive logical inferences or final conclusions are drawn. The text only documents observable phenomena, presuppositions and unresolved open questions about human aesthetic perception. The observation covers multiple dimensions: Contrast between continuous natural aesthetic ontology and discretized, standardized man-made representations under industrialization, market economy and educational indoctrination; Prerequisites for delicate aesthetic contemplation: mental quietude, cognitive knowledge support and release from urgent survival pressure; Correlation between survival anxiety and the capacity for fine aesthetic observation, illustrated through selected historical cases, with explicit caveats that these are partial examples without universal generalization; Distinction between extrinsic objective aesthetic stimuli (subject to biological sensory fatigue) and intrinsic subjective aesthetic experience (cumulative and growing); Two-layer mechanism for human beauty judgment: innate perceptual instinct and acquired learned evaluation criteria. The manuscript puts forward an open proposition: aesthetic cultivation relies on quietude for contemplation, knowledge for reflective thinking, authenticity to restrain illusory perception, and relaxed non-survival-oriented mental space to nurture endogenous aesthetic sensibility. All statements are reserved as open-ended observations. The complete formation mechanism of aesthetic perception remains undetermined for further continued observation. This work follows the A00: Five Ways · One Law human-AI collaborative original work attribution paradigm.

The emergence of Generation Z has coincided with major changes in education, communication, technology and social life. Students of this generation learn in an environment shaped by smartphones, social media, digital platforms, online resources and increasingly, generative artificial intelligence (AI). These developments have expanded access to information and created opportunities for personalized and innovative learning, but have also introduced challenges such as distraction, information overload, social comparison, digital well-being concerns and academic pressure. The present paper examines the educational implications of Generation Z in relation to digital culture, educational innovation and social transformation, while drawing upon an earlier empirical study of anxiety and academic achievement among 400 XII-grade students in Jamshedpur. The sample consisted of 200 Arts and 200 Science students preparing for the ISC Board Examination. Anxiety was examined through Examination, Social, Personal and Family Anxiety, while academic achievement was assessed through pre-board examination marks. The findings indicate predominantly moderate anxiety in both groups. No significant differences were found between Arts and Science students in Examination and Social Anxiety, whereas significant differences were found in Personal and Family Anxiety. A significant difference was also reported in academic achievement, with Arts students obtaining a higher mean score than Science students. The paper reinterprets these findings in the contemporary context of Generation Z without claiming that digital technology caused the reported anxiety. It argues that meaningful educational transformation requires a balanced ecosystem combining digital

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) enables students with little programming experience to produce working software, raising the concern that learners may build artifacts they cannot explain. This convergent mixed-methods study examined how uncritical GenAI use and verification behavior (VB) relate to novices’ self-reported understanding of their own AI-assisted projects. Participants were undergraduates from predominantly non-computing majors in two offerings of a general-education Python course; 64 provided complete survey data and 68 written reflections were thematically analyzed. Uncritical use (UR) was associated with a larger self-reported product–understanding gap (GAP; r = 0.43, p < 0.001) but showed little association with perceived understanding (PU), whereas VB was associated with PU (r = 0.45, p < 0.001) but showed little association with the gap. Tests of dependent correlations confirmed that these associations differed. In the reflections, execution-based checking was the most commonly reported verification strategy (47 of 68), whereas comprehension-oriented strategies were less common. Because all measures were self-reported and cross-sectional, the findings are correlational; they suggest that instruction should explicitly scaffold comprehension-oriented verification in AI-integrated introductory programming.

In the twenty-first century, digital technology brought about extensive changes in the nature, process, and objectives of education. Moving beyond traditional teacher-centered and classroom-centered teaching, education is now advancing towards online learning, blended learning, smart classrooms, mobile learning, digital teaching resources, and artificial intelligence (AI)-based teaching. In this context, Generation Z students are particularly important because their social and educational environment has developed alongside digital technologies. Technological media has made the teaching-learning process more flexible, participatory, and student-centered. Generation Z is the generation that has grown up with digital technologies. Thus, digital education innovation is not merely a means of modernizing the teaching process; it is also an important means of developing technological literacy among students. The objective of this conceptual research paper is to clarify the conceptual relationship between digital education innovation and technological literacy with reference to Generation Z students. In this study, digital education innovation is viewed as an educational process in which digital devices, online teaching, AI-based technologies, digital resources, and innovative teaching methods are effectively used. Technological literacy refers to students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and to employ technological devices and digital resources safely and responsibly. This paper argues that effective digital education innovation can provide a strong foundation for students’ technological competence, digital problem-solving ability, information evaluation ability, and digital citizenship. At the same time, it is necessary to pay attention to challenges such as the digital divide, technological inequality, digital safety, teacher training, availability of technological resources, misinformation, privacy, cybersecurity, and uncontrolled use of artificial intelligence.

This article presents a comparative analysis of existing software and hardware solutions used in training simulators for man-portable air-defense system operators. The study examines the main features of the Stinger Simulator, I-STPTv2, Igla-2 Trainer, and 9F635M1 field simulator based on available technical information. Particular attention is given to simulator functionality, instructor control, virtual environments, data collection, performance assessment, and system flexibility. Based on the comparative analysis, a modular intelligent training simulator architecture for the QW-18 system is proposed. The proposed architecture consists of six interconnected functional modules organized into three main layers. The study also considers the potential application of artificial intelligence for analyzing training results and supporting individual learning. The proposed approach provides a theoretical and methodological basis for the further development and evaluation of modern training simulators.

Personalized recommendation under uncertain user preferences and conflicting multi-criteria constraints poses a fundamental challenge in decision support systems. This study proposes a framework integrating fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making (FMCDM) with ant colony optimization (ACO). The framework contributes three components: a Mamdani-type fuzzy inference engine transforming linguistic preferences into priority scores across four criteria; an FMCDM-enhanced ACO algorithm embedding fuzzy scoring into transition probabilities for route optimization; and an adaptive inference mechanism recalibrating recommendation depth based on behavioral signals. The framework is evaluated through Monte Carlo simulation using the Rijksmuseum dataset (60 artifacts). Simulation across 7500 synthetic trajectories suggests 15.5% higher path efficiency than TOPSIS-based baselines under modeled conditions (criteria balance SD: 0.033 vs. 0.171). A preliminary expert assessment with twelve museum professionals (N = 12) provides exploratory evidence that human–AI collaborative content approaches human-authored quality at substantially reduced production time.

Emotion regulation is a key construct in mental health, yet existing measures differ in conceptual coverage, with some focusing on specific strategies or regulatory difficulties rather than broader cognitive, behavioral, and contextual regulation processes. This study aimed to develop an Emotion Regulation Scale (ERS) grounded in Gross’s Process Model, using large language models (LLMs) as assistive tools within an established psychometric framework. This cross-sectional study included 743 adults recruited through convenience sampling. Participants were randomly divided into two non-overlapping subsamples, one used for exploratory factor analysis and the other for confirmatory factor analysis. Multiple LLMs and AI-based tools assisted with item generation, refinement and bias screening, translation, and post-EFA construct interpretation, with human oversight throughout development. An initial pool of 25 items was generated and refined to produce the final 17-item ERS. The ERS revealed a preliminary four-factor structure, with EFA explaining 50.85% of the variance. CFA provided preliminary support for a post hoc refined 17-item model (χ²/df = 1.95, CFI = 0.934, TLI = 0.918, IFI = 0.935, RMSEA = 0.050). Reliability was acceptable for early-stage scale development (α = 0.68–0.74; ω = 0.68–0.75). Convergent validity showed positive correlations between adaptive strategies and cognitive reappraisal ( r = 0.522–0.608) and between maladaptive cognitions and suppression ( r = 0.400). Concurrent validity showed associations with depression ( r = 0.432), anxiety ( r = 0.462), well-being ( r = -0.330), and quality of life (QOL1 = -0.357; QOL2 = -0.295), while adaptive strategies correlated with depression ( r = -0.184 to -0.239), anxiety ( r = -0.141 to -0.211), well-being ( r = 0.150 to 0.203), and quality of life ( r = 0.211 to 0.375). Known-groups validity indicated significant differences across depression and anxiety levels (MCR: F(4, 738) = 39.32; 64.49, p < 0.001). The findings provide preliminary psychometric evidence for the 17-item ERS and suggest that it may complement existing measures by capturing broader cognitive, behavioral, and contextual emotion regulation processes. The study illustrates the potential for LLM-assisted scale development within established psychometric procedures and human oversight. Further research using diverse samples is needed to evaluate the scale’s psychometric properties, generalizability, and broader utility.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: Abstract Healthcare workers (HCWs) face infection risks through patient care, specimen processing, sharps, contaminated environments, and exposures outside healthcare settings. Vulnerability was illustrated during COVID-19, when the World Health Organization estimated that 80,000–180,000 health and care workers could have died from COVID-19 between January 2020 and May 2021. This narrative review examines role-specific exposure pathways, barriers to adherence to infection prevention and control (IPC) measures, and strategies for reducing occupational and community-acquired infections among HCWs. English-language sources published during 2015–2025 were identified through targeted database and public-health-agency searches, last updated 30 June 2026. Evidence was organized thematically by HCW role, transmission route, barrier, and preventive intervention. Occupational risk was concentrated in aerosol-generating procedures, dental drilling, airway management, specimen centrifugation, direct contact with lesions or body fluids, sharps injuries, and contaminated equipment or surfaces. Recurrent barriers included inadequate training, personal protective equipment (PPE) shortages or poor fit, workload, staffing deficiencies, emergency time pressure, weak safety culture, and inconsistent institutional enforcement, with resource limitations especially influential in low- and middle-income settings. Community respiratory and household exposures may cause workforce infection and contribute to subsequent transmission within healthcare settings. Effective protection therefore requires standard precautions, transmission-based precautions, vaccination, safe sharps systems, engineering and environmental controls, adequate staffing, continuous competency-based training, and leadership accountability. Protecting HCWs should be treated as both an occupational-health obligation and a patient-safety strategy; interventions should be adapted to task-specific risks and local resources rather than relying on PPE alone.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This paper proposes a new approach to managing the human factor within an occupational safety management system. The approach is based on viewing the human factor as the interaction between two complex nonlinear dynamic systems: “human characteristics” and “working conditions.” The authors introduce a quantitative assessment of the human factor by comparing the worker’s actual set of abilities–intellectual, sensory, protective, and physical–with the required set of abilities determined by the working conditions. A model of a personal occupational safety management system has been developed. This system forms part of an individual’s self-management system and is responsible for preserving the worker’s life and health. A method for assessing the effectiveness of this system is also proposed, based on the difference between the actual and required abilities to manage personal occupational safety measures. Based on the proposed model, a technology for continuous rapid workplace training has been developed. It is aimed at forming sustainable safe-behavior skills among workers. The paper presents an analysis of the results of implementing this technology at industrial enterprises, which demonstrated a 1.5- to 3-fold reduction in occupational injuries over a period of one to two years. It was established that workers displaying a safe type of behavior experience occupational injuries eight times less frequently than those displaying unsafe behavior. The authors conclude that the proposed approach is highly effective in practice as a tool for the large-scale development of safe behavior.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study develops a safety-aware supervisory framework for industrial fed-batch bioreactors by integrating an adaptive digital twin, fuzzy multi-objective optimization, Agentic LLM reasoning, and an independent Safety Governor within a closed-loop architecture. The digital twin continuously reconstructs process states and updates sensitive parameters, while α-cut fuzzy intervals preserve biological and operational uncertainty throughout prediction and optimization. The Agentic LLM coordinates prediction, optimization, process knowledge, and candidate evaluation, and supports context-dependent reevaluation and replanning as operating conditions evolve. The framework was evaluated using data from 12 industrial 72 h fed-batch runs, together with 600 uncertainty-aware simulated trajectories. Across three fully independent validation batches, the digital twin achieved an average NRMSE of 4.7%, MAPE of 4.4%, and R2 of 0.985. Closed-loop operation achieved a volumetric productivity of 0.347 g/L·h while maintaining a positive minimum dissolved-oxygen margin of 5 percentage points and zero hard-constraint violations. Across nominal and stressed scenarios, the Safety Governor preserved feasible operation with no residual hard-constraint violations, while the Agentic LLM successfully activated reevaluation and replanning following changes in process conditions. The ablation results further showed that the complete architecture provided the strongest overall balance among productivity, biological risk, robustness, and disturbance recovery. These findings demonstrate the value of combining adaptive process representation, uncertainty-aware optimization, agentic supervisory reasoning, and independent safety validation for reliable intelligent bioprocess operation.

As electric vehicle (EV) adoption grows, improving EV charging management depends on accurate forecasts of charging demand and station occupancy, along with effective route guidance and dynamic charging-selection policies. Yet many existing approaches address only one component and do not provide an end-to-end pipeline that handles multiple goals. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a sequential, multi-stage framework that predicts EV charging volume and occupancy under dynamic conditions while simultaneously optimising objectives such as routing, congestion, and cost. For forecasting, the framework uses an LSTM–Transformer model to learn both local and global dependencies and to deliver multi-horizon predictions. For optimisation, it applies reinforcement learning with proximal policy optimisation (RL-PPO), improving decisions by utilising a predicted feature map. In addition, the forecasting signals and agent outputs are leveraged to produce interpretable, LLM-based explanations, helping users to better understand the model’s predictions. The framework is evaluated on diverse datasets, including urban networks from two public benchmarks (UrbanEV and Multi-Faceted) and custom data from the Al Jouf region in Saudi Arabia. The results demonstrate the model’s effectiveness, achieving minimum RMSE values of 0.3244, 0.9339, and 0.15, with predictions closely matching the observed signals. In the optimisation stage, the proposed RL-PPO method achieves the best performance across all three datasets in terms of distance (km), congestion, and waiting time, resulting in higher customer satisfaction and a stronger trade-off than competing methods. Overall, the study delivers accurate forecasting, optimised decision support, and human-readable explanations, enabling an intelligent EV charging system.

The increasing use of various types of probabilistic AI technologies in decision-making roles limits the usefulness of traditional business analysis and design (B&A) methods for documenting non-AI decision-makers and other aspects of probabilistic AI systems‚ including human backup decision-making roles․ Traditional UML and other business analysis tools support only binary decision outcomes and offer few tools for documenting the shared decision-making responsibilities of AI and human decision makers․ This paper proposes an AI-Socio B&A method that integrates traditional business analysis methods with three new tools:(1) a Confidence-Based Delegation Matrix offering three levels of AI decision-making authority (automatic decision making when confidence exceeds 80%‚ assisted decision making when confidence is between 50% and 80%‚ and human backup decision making when confidence is below 50%); (2) an amended use case format that offers additional documentation of confidence levels and bias-prevention techniques along with other information; (3) a process for obtaining and using feedback from human decision makers to improve the AI system․ A case study of an AI-Powered Job Applicant Screening and Short-listing System‚ including documentation of an extended use case (UC-02)‚ actors matrix‚ two design diagrams‚ and comparison with traditional B&A and UML documentation on five design and safety metrics‚ illustrates use of the new AI-Socio B&A method․ Advantages of AI-Socio B&A include reduced automation bias and inclusion of anonymization as a requirement and other tools to share work between human and AI decision makers․
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence technology is gradually being integrated into mental health service contexts and is increasingly discussed as a potential supplementary resource to university mental health support systems. However, AI-based mental health services involve sensitive factors such as emotional expression, personal privacy, and relational interaction. Therefore, college students’ willingness to accept AI-based mental health services and the potential factors associated with such acceptance remain unclear. Based on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, this study introduces six factors—Accessibility (ACC), Privacy Concern (PC), Perceived Anthropomorphism (PA), Perceived Empathy (EMP), Trust (TRU), and Perceived Usefulness (PU)—to systematically examine their relationships with university students’ Behavioral Intention (BI) to use AI-based mental health services. A total of 375 volunteers participated in the current study and completed relevant questionnaires. Structural equation modeling was employed for data analysis. The results indicate that accessibility, perceived usefulness, and trust are all significantly and positively associated with behavioral intention. Perceived empathy is significantly and positively associated with trust, whereas privacy concern is significantly and negatively associated with both trust and behavioral intention. The analysis of indirect effects shows that there is a significant sequential indirect association between perceived anthropomorphism and behavioral intention through perceived empathy, trust, and perceived usefulness. In addition, a significant negative indirect association between privacy concern and behavioral intention through trust was observed. The findings indicate that, in the highly sensitive context of mental health services, college students’ intention to use AI-based mental health services is associated with a combination of accessibility, perceived usefulness, emotional interaction experience, privacy-related evaluations, and trust.

The extensive usage of AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini, has led to a complete transformation of the ways young people acquire information, conduct their academic assignments, and perform technical tasks. However, with the rise in popularity of these platforms, worries emerge regarding the protection of users' information while exchanging it on these sites. The purpose of this study is to identify the degree of awareness regarding the problem of data privacy among young people who use AI chatbots in the state of Maharashtra. The descriptive approach was applied in the research process, and primary data were collected through the use of Google Forms surveys. The sample consisted of 151 respondents aged 15-29 who utilized AI chatbots and exchanged personal information, privacy measures, risks, knowledge about the storage and training of the model, and data protection laws. Some of the AI systems that were in common usage include ChatGPT and Google Gemini, while the type of information that was in widespread sharing included academic information. However, there is one other important observation on the lack of privacy settings, the lack of awareness of storing conversations, and also the limited self-reported awareness of the Indian Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 or similar data laws. The findings of this research suggest the need for proper digital privacy education, clear privacy information in different languages, proper data sharing, and awareness programs.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Hou-Hsun Liao,1– 3 Yu-Sheng Liu,1 Ying-To Hsu,4 Ming-Hsien Yeh,1 Szu-Chin Li,5,6 Tzung-Yi Tsai7,81Department of Chinese Medicine, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan; 2Department of Biochemical Science and Technology, College of Life Sciences, National Chiayi University, Chiayi City, Taiwan; 3Master Program in Integrated Medicine and Pharmacy Science, College of Life Sciences, National Chiayi University, Chiayi City, Taiwan; 4Division of Allergy, Immunology and Rheumatology, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan; 5School of Medicine, Tzu Chi University, Hualien, Taiwan; 6Division of Hematology and Oncology, Department of Internal Medicine, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, Taiwan; 7Department of Environmental and Occupational Health, College of Medicine, National Cheng Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan; 8Department of Medical Research, Dalin Tzu Chi Hospital, Buddhist Tzu Chi Medical Foundation, Chiayi, TaiwanCorrespondence: Szu-Chin Li; Tzung-Yi Tsai, Email lisrau@gmail.com; dm732024@tzuchi.com.twBackground: Systemic chemotherapy increases the risk of thrombocytopenia in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML), which may lead to risk of bleeding and treatment interruption. Accumulating evidence indicates that traditional Chinese medicinal herbs (TCMH) may accelerate symptom relief. We hypothesized that integrating TCMH alongside standard treatment may decrease the risk of chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia (CIT) in patients with AML.Aim: To compare the likelihood of CIT among patients with AML who received adjunctive TCMH plus standard treatment and those who received standard treatment alone.Methods: This nested case–control study analyzed individuals aged 20 and older who were newly diagnosed with AML, had no pre-existing CIT, and were identified from the Taiwan National Health Insurance Research Database between 2002 and 2010. Five controls were then randomly matched to each CIT case from the remaining eligible cohort. All participants were followed until December 31, 2013. Conditional logistic regression was used to assess the association between TCMH use and risk of developing CIT.Results: TCMH was prescribed in 5.5% of cases and 20.6% of controls. Combining TCMH treatment with standard therapy substantially reduced risk of CIT (OR= 0.21; 95% CI:0.11– 0.39). The inverse association between adjunctive TCMH use and CIT was strongest among patients who received TCMH for more than 180 days. Age and gender did not influence the association between TCMH use and the risk of CIT.Conclusion: The current research emphasized the importance of framing a collaborative healthcare model for AML persons, especially involvement of TCMH, to effectively manage the poor complications that arise from cancer therapy.Keywords: acute myeloid leukemia, chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia, traditional Chinese medicinal herbs, nested case–control study, chemotherapy

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to make water management more intuitive through natural language interfaces. However, the generalised training of these models limits their effectiveness at domain-specific tasks such as stormwater modelling, particularly when nuanced answers require executing and modifying water models. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) addresses this challenge by providing a standardised interface for LLMs to interact with external tools while enforcing guardrails for quality control. Building on this protocol, we introduce SWMM-MCP, a cross-platform, model agnostic framework that enables conversational interaction with the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s Stormwater Management Model (EPA SWMM). SWMM-MCP leverages the swmm_api and PySWMM libraries through an MCP server built with FAST-MCP, allowing users to configure, modify, and evaluate SWMM models via natural language. We demonstrate SWMM-MCP using a benchmark task and prompt-response evaluations comparing performance using eight different base LLMs. For the benchmark SWMM task, all base LLMs completed the tasks, but at varying levels of computational efficiency and detailed responses. For the prompt-response evaluations, the LLMs exhibited distinct personalities. Results highlight that even within a structured MCP framework, LLM selection significantly affects task efficiency and domain specific prompting remains important for optimal performance.

ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed smart surveillance systems, significantly leveraging technologies such as deep learning, computer vision, and adaptive monitoring. Driven by the need for real‐time object detection, behavioral analysis, and automated alerting, AI‐powered surveillance is increasingly vital for enhancing public safety, operational efficiency, and decision‐making in fields such as security, health‐care, transportation, and environmental monitoring. The growing societal impact and complexity of surveillance necessitate a comprehensive examination of foundational methodologies, key application domains, and the technical, ethical, and operational challenges associated with these systems. Analysis reveals that although AI‐driven surveillance solutions offer improved accuracy, scalability, and responsiveness, they continue to face notable barriers including high computational demands, privacy and data quality concerns, interpretability limitations, and inadequate regulatory frameworks. The review further identifies critical emerging trends, such as sustainable AI practices, human‐AI collaborative models, and the integration of AI with the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain technologies, as significant influences shaping the future trajectory of the field. Addressing these challenges through ongoing research, innovation, and responsible deployment is essential to fully unlock the societal and industrial potential of AI‐enabled surveillance solutions.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Mobile and application-derived artefacts are becoming more central to digital forensic investigations; however, they can be a diverse set of evidence in a UFDR which are hard to prioritize manually. Mobile and application derived-artifacts are becoming more important to digital forensic investigations, and can be a diverse set of evidence in a UFDR that is difficult to manually prioritize. In the paper, the authors propose an Artificial Intelligence-based UFDR report analysis and intelligent digital forensic investigation assistant to transform the extracted report information into a structured and explainable analysis flow. The prototype now supports reading reports in JSON, XML, CSV and ZIP formats, validates the uploaded report, calculates an integrity checksum (SHA-256), and stores proof of the integrity in SQLite. Twenty behavioral features are created in communication, temporal, browser, application, and file activity. The trained Random Forest (RF) classifier enables three-way classification, and a trained Isolation Forest (Anomaly scoring) is used. A suspicious detector based on the 4 parameters is set, and activates when late-night activity is detected, or when suspicious incoming/outgoing communication, suspicious text indicators or high anomaly scores are detected. The conditions are combined using UNION logic and deduplicated by evidence identifier to return suspicious and/or critical records to the investigators. Risk engine helps transform the model and indicator outputs are mapped to a 0-100 score, and with the help of SHAP Tree Explainer, it is possible to get feature contributions by the model and a human-readable “WHY?” explanation based on evidence. An evidence-based assistant retrieves case, analysis and explanation information from the database and provides a deterministic answer when the language-model service is not available. The accuracy of the test split was 93% and F1-score, recall and macro precision were all approximately 0.93 for the synthetic benchmark that was reproduced using the project. Suspicious-detector tests were also conducted successfully, with special emphasis on specific tests. This system instead of the automatic finding of criminal conduct presents a non-automatic triage system, explainability and a conversational workflow for forensic decision support.

Haul trucks generate more than half of direct greenhouse-gas emissions in typical mining operations, making haulage decarbonization central to the industry’s net zero commitments. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to haulage, but existing reviews examine individual technologies rather than linking them to decarbonization and ESG outcomes. This comprehensive review synthesizes 73 peer-reviewed sources from 2017 to 2026 across route optimization, electric and hybrid trucks, predictive maintenance, fleet monitoring, carbon footprint reduction, and ESG performance, grades reported outcomes by validation basis, and develops a framework linking AI-enabled technology domains, through their operational mechanisms, to ESG outcomes. Reinforcement-learning dispatching reduced haulage emissions by more than 30% relative to fixed scheduling in simulation, trolley assist reduced fuel use by up to 91%, and fleet electrification modeling projected GHG reductions of up to 92.6% in a hypothetical case, contingent on grid carbon intensity. Most reported reductions derive from simulation, and AI’s advantage over conventional control of electrified fleets remains undemonstrated. Gaps include scarce field-verified emission baselines, limited modeling of operator behavior, immature cybersecurity and data governance practice, and weak engagement between ESG research and haulage technology. AI-enabled operational measures offer a promising near-term decarbonization pathway that complements, rather than awaits, fleet electrification.
