documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being investigated as a means to advance forensic histopathology from visual description to quantitative mapping, pattern recognition, and multimodal reconstruction of death. Recent developments in human postmortem analysis include validated whole-slide digitisation as foundational infrastructure and task-specific AI applications for diatom detection, glomerular quantification, coronary morphometry, myocardial classification, immunohistochemistry scoring, and virtual staining. AI-based postmortem interval (PMI) estimation remains experimental; the multi-organ study referenced in this commentary utilised an animal model, and human forensic validity has not yet been established. Foundation and vision-language models may ultimately extend these capabilities across organs and integrate microscopic findings with autopsy, toxicological, radiological, and circumstantial evidence. Postmortem tissue, however, is subject to autolysis, decomposition, agonal events, resuscitation, and non-standardised sampling, while the reference diagnosis is often a probabilistic whole-case opinion rather than an objective slide label. This work introduces FORENS-AI (FORensic Histopathology Evidence Network and Safeguards for AI), a conceptual architecture designed to convert computational outputs into traceable medicolegal evidence. FORENS-AI has not been empirically validated and is not presented as a standard, scoring system, clinical decision rule, or practice recommendation. The framework represents findings as an evidence graph, separates the Slide, Case, and Claim Gates, and proposes progressively stronger validation as outputs move from measurement to temporal, mechanistic, or causal inference. The primary aim is not to automate certification of death, but to identify safeguards to evaluate before AI-derived histological findings are permitted to inform expert opinion.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The contemporary media industry is undergoing one of the most profound transformations in the history of mass communication. Digital platforms, social networks, mobile technologies, big data, algorithmic distribution systems and, most recently, generative artificial intelligence have fundamentally changed the production, distribution and consumption of information. The traditional model in which professional media institutions controlled the principal channels of information has evolved into a complex digital ecosystem where journalists, media organisations, technology platforms, bloggers, influencers, artificial intelligence systems and ordinary users simultaneously participate in the creation and circulation of content. This article examines the transformation of mass media in the context of digitalisation, technological innovation and the rapid development of artificial intelligence. Particular attention is paid to the integration of generative AI into newsroom processes, including information gathering, transcription, translation, data analysis, content production, fact-checking, personalisation and audience engagement. The study argues that artificial intelligence should not be interpreted merely as an instrument of automation. Rather, it represents a structural factor capable of changing journalistic workflows, professional competencies, editorial responsibility, media economics and the relationship between media institutions and their audiences. At the same time, AI-driven journalism generates significant professional and ethical risks, including algorithmic bias, hallucinated information, deepfakes, synthetic content, copyright disputes and the possible erosion of public trust. The article concludes that the future competitiveness and social legitimacy of media organisations will depend not simply on technological adoption, but on their ability to combine innovation with professional standards, human editorial oversight, transparency and accountability.

Presentation at the 21st Annual Conference of the European Society for Textual Scholarship (ESTS 2026), Lublin, Poland. 30.05.2026. Abstract: Machine learning and artificial intelligence open new possibilities for dealing with large text corpora, where content structuring becomes essential because readers can no longer grasp the corpus through close reading alone. We think that approaches such as topic modeling or AI-based keyword assignment in digital editions can help address this challenge. Building on Hans Zeller’s foundational distinction between record (Befund) and interpretation (Deutung) (Zeller 1971), we argue that these computational approaches constitute a new layer of record. Although their analytical character may suggest an interpretive element, systematic and transparent documentation ensures that they do not exceed the interpretive scope inherent in any editorial practice (Martens 1994, S. 74; Sahle 2013, S. 210). Like qualitative editorial findings, this computational record may contain biases and opacities, which underscores the need for transparent documentation (Henny-Krahmer, Neuber 2014). Yet these methods could offer a curatorial angle, offering perspectives that can encourage editors to reassess their own biases and assumptions. By exposing patterns beyond the reach of close reading, they enhance the accessibility of the material and temporarily complement the editor’s work, offering additional interpretive pathways. Using the digital edition of Jean Paul's letters (Bernauer et al. 2018) as a case study (ca. 12,000 documents), we demonstrate how computational methods for content analysis can be integrated into editorial data models and interfaces. We will focus particularly on the interplay between computational findings (which remain record) and their interpretation (which requires human scholarly judgment); a relationship which we conceive as complementary rather than hierarchical.

The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has unsettled long standing assumptions about the validity, reliability, and authenticity of conventional assessment methods. Existing research has predominantly examined perceptions, ethical concerns, and technology acceptance, leaving the actual pedagogical redesign work of faculty, and its relationship to established principles of assessment quality, comparatively underexplored. Drawing on constructive alignment theory, this study examines how faculty are reshaping assessment design under conditions of AI disruption and whether their adaptation strategies address or fail to address core dimensions of assessment validity. A sequential explanatory mixed methods design was used across two phases: a survey of 180 faculty members across STEM and non STEM disciplines at a private institution in India, followed by semi structured interviews and assessment artefact analysis with a purposively selected subset of participants. The results show a marked shift away from unsupervised, product based assessment toward process oriented, reflective, and authentic formats, including oral examinations, project based tasks, in class problem solving, and reflective journals, an implicit faculty led re alignment of assessment with intended learning outcomes. Faculty frame GenAI simultaneously as a threat to assessment integrity and as a catalyst for pedagogical innovation, but institutional structures have not kept pace with this bottom up change, and increased workload, inconsistent guidance, and limited professional development persist as barriers to sustaining and scaling redesign. By empirically documenting faculty led transformation and connecting it explicitly to theories of assessment quality and institutional change, the study moves beyond descriptive accounts of GenAI's impact and offers practical guidance for educators, instructional designers, and institutional leaders seeking to formalise sustainable, valid, and equitable assessment redesign in the GenAI era.

Leveraging auxiliary textual data can help with user profiling and item characterization in recommender systems (RSs). However, incomplete user and item descriptions limit the potential of textual information. To this end, we propose a graph-aware convolutional large language model (LLM) method, eliciting LLMs to summarize from a high-order interaction graph to generate fine-grained descriptions for users and items. We focus on two challenges in this paper: 1) the incompatibility between structural graph and text-aware LLMs . Although some work converts graph data into textual form using templates and sampling strategies, they limit the LLMs’ ability to maintain a global perspective on graphs for LLM reasoning. 2) the limitation of LLMs’ capability for long context. Simply describing a large-scale graph in a textual format makes LLM struggle to robustly comprehend information from lengthy contextual inputs. To bridge the gap between graph structures and LLMs, we employ the LLM as an aggregator for the graph convolution process, eliciting it to aggregate and refine the graph-based information iteratively. To mitigate the information overload associated with large-scale graphs, we segment the graph processing into manageable steps, progressively incorporating multi-hop information in a least-to-most manner. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches.

Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involves practical literacy as well as learning, professional, sociotechnical, and configuration concerns. This mixed-methods study examined whether these responses were differentiated among Chinese arts-university students. Primary inference used a quality-screened cross-sectional sample of 355 questionnaire records from 351 participant-identifier clusters after excluding 105 of 460 eligible records (22.8%) showing exact whole-battery straightlining across all 59 structured items; the full eligible sample of 460 records from 455 clusters was retained as a sensitivity analysis. GenAI literacy was assessed with a 16-item music-context-adapted self-report instrument covering cognitive (CL), behavioral (BL), affective (AL), and ethical (EL) literacy, and AI Anxiety with 21 items spanning Learning Anxiety (LA), Job-Replacement Anxiety (JR), Sociotechnical Blindness Anxiety (ST), and AI Configuration Anxiety (AC). Of six prespecified associations, only EL-JR and EL-ST met the Holm-adjusted criterion in the primary sample and remained supported in the full-sample and prior-use-adjusted sensitivity analyses. CL-LA and BL-LA were unsupported in both samples, whereas AL-LA and AL-AC were sample-specification sensitive. Measurement models showed mixed fit; CL-BL separation improved after quality screening but remained incomplete. A secondary 47-person exact-identifier matched panel showed higher later-wave CL, BL, and AL scores, whereas EL and all four AI Anxiety dimensions showed no Holm-adjusted difference. These literacy comparisons are exploratory because the administered literacy items were music-framed while the documented learning activities involved broadcasting scripts and AI-supported video production. Independently analyzed qualitative material provided construct-level consistency with the EL-ST interpretation and tentative complementarity for EL-JR, but was not participant-linked to the quantitative samples. Overall, the evidence supports a bounded interpretation of differentiated, calibrated rather than anxiety-free adaptation; it does not establish causal intervention effects or participant-level mixed-method mechanisms.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming routine in university study, yet institutional responses often separate technical fluency, academic integrity, and responsible governance. This integrative conceptual synthesis develops governance-aware GenAI literacy for adult higher education. A bounded, purposive review of 28 sources published through 10 September 2026 combined peer-reviewed studies, foundational scholarship, policy frameworks, and one preprint. Sources were coded for learning capability, epistemic risk, pedagogical mechanism, governance requirement, and strength of evidence. The resulting framework comprises five connected domains: epistemic verification, task and interaction specification, dialogic reflection, ethical governance, and transfer to professional action, all centred on visible human accountability. The framework extends beyond text prompting to multimodal, personalised, and agentic systems. It is translated into a pilot-ready eight-week sequence, tiered workload model, assessment evidence, accessibility safeguards, disciplinary adaptations, and an evaluation protocol. The paper does not claim empirical validation of the model or optimality of the sequence. Instead, it offers a bounded design proposition for testing. Governance-aware literacy is presented as the capacity to use AI productively while documenting, verifying, contesting, and justifying its contribution in academic and professional contexts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Explaining anomalies in spatiotemporal data requires more than identifying statistical deviations; it often demands coherent narratives that relate events to their spatial, temporal, and social context. In urban settings, where anomalies may reflect public events, behavioral shifts, or environmental factors, the lack of interpretable, contextual explanations limits the effectiveness of automated analysis. We present GroundSTory , an interactive framework that reframes spatiotemporal anomaly explanation as computational storytelling, integrating graph-based representations of urban space, coordinated visual analytics, and large language models (LLMs) to support the construction of grounded, human-readable narrative explanations. Anomalies act as narrative anchors, while localized spatial and temporal relations and contextual signals derived from the graph guide and constrain narrative generation. The LLM functions as a narrative assistant, proposing plausible, evidence-backed hypotheses that analysts can inspect, compare, and validate through visual interaction. We illustrate the approach through qualitative usage scenarios on real-world urban datasets from São Paulo and New York City, showing how interactive narratives surface meaningful links between detected anomalies and contextual factors such as holidays, mass events, and routine activity patterns. A prompt analysis further suggests that structured, graph-derived context tends to affect the stability and perceived quality of generated hypotheses. Overall, our results indicate that combining knowledge-driven representations, interactive visualization, and constrained prompting can support more coherent, plausible, and interpretable narratives for spatiotemporal anomaly analysis, contributing to ongoing research in interactive storytelling and narrative-centered AI systems.

Human demonstrations can capture task-relevant manipulation without using the target robot, but the recorded hand motions cannot directly serve as robot action supervision. Hand reconstruction and motion retargeting provide a direct route to such supervision, yet recovering hand motion alone does not ensure physically consistent hand-object interactions. To address this issue, we introduce Hand2Robot, an object-centric 4D hand reconstruction framework for robot policy post-training. Given videos of humans performing the target task, Hand2Robot extracts interaction clips, reconstructs object geometry, and generates robot action supervision through hand-object interaction optimization and motion retargeting. For object tracking, we combine observation confidence with temporal motion constraints to select a globally consistent object pose trajectory from per-frame pose candidates. For hand refinement, we use object geometry and motion as a reference and combine staged 2D alignment with object-local contact constraints to refine hand trajectories and finger joint configurations. Experiments on DexYCB and HO3D-v3 show improved object pose accuracy and hand-object interaction quality. Experiments on three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks further show that reconstructed and retargeted human demonstrations can effectively supplement limited robot data for target-task policy post-training.

Purpose: This chapter looks at how artificial intelligence (AI) can enable sustainable financial activities, especially in terms of risk assessment, optimisation of investment, and compliance with regulation to promote healthy, inclusive financial systems. Need for the study: Finance and sustainable finance are reshaping the world markets as the sustainability issues of the environment, social, and governance (ESG) increase, but the difficulties of data biases, ethical issues, and regulatory uncertainties remain. AI integration applies to these by improving ESG ratings, climate risk analysis, and impact investments and growing the industry to $2.5 trillion. Methodology: The review of AI-based technologies, including machine learning (ML), natural language processing (NLP), and big data analytics, is conducted and reviewed in the context of their use in the ESG scoring, carbon footprint estimation, and predictive climate forecasting based on the case studies of the global financial institutions. Findings: AI generates better financial returns in ESG portfolios compared to traditional ones, enhances transparency in sustainability, reduces fraud, and allows accurate predictive instruments on climate event risks to support green bond strategies. Practical implications: Researchers of AI and policymakers, as well as institutions, should cooperate in order to limit bias and ethical concerns, enabling equitable adoption of AI to support sustainable robust finance.

Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare, primarily supporting clinical decision-making. Agentic AI may extend these applications by autonomously planning, coordinating, and executing clinical and administrative workflows. However, empirical evidence on how healthcare professionals conceptualise agentic AI and anticipate its implications for work and occupational well-being remains limited. This study explores healthcare professionals’ perceptions and expectations regarding agentic AI and its potential effects on healthcare work. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 25 healthcare professionals from different clinical backgrounds in Germany. Interviews explored perceptions of agentic AI, focusing on workflow organisation, workload, professional autonomy, accountability, and occupational well-being. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. Results: Five themes were identified: (1) from assisting decisions to organising work; (2) automation redistributes rather than removes work; (3) delegating action without delegating responsibility; (4) implications for working conditions and health- and work-related outcomes; and (5) meaningful human control requires organisational conditions. Participants distinguished between conventional AI-based decision support and more autonomous forms of AI in their accounts, using this contrast to describe potential changes in workflow organisation. Their accounts highlighted practical consequences of delegating workflow-related activities to AI systems, including changes in task structures, monitoring and verification demands, exception management, and the distribution of professional responsibility. Participants anticipated reduced routine administrative workload and improved care coordination, but also potential increases in cognitive and supervisory demands. Conclusions: Agentic AI may shift healthcare from AI-assisted decision-making towards AI-mediated workflow execution. Its effects on occupational well-being may therefore be bidirectional, combining workload relief with increased cognitive and supervisory demands. Appropriate governance, clearly defined accountability, meaningful human oversight, workforce training, and regulatory alignment will be essential for responsible implementation.

documents.abstract: This study investigates degrees of polarization in political climate protest debates on TikTok. Drawing on a dataset of automatically transcribed TikTok videos posted by German politicians between 2022 and 2025 (N ≈ 1,700), alongside associated user comments (N ≈ 53,000), this study compares discussions on general climate activism, reformist activism (Fridays for Future), and disruptive activism (Letzte Generation). Using a mixed-method approach that combines Large Language Model-based frame classification, stance detection, and network analysis, this study operationalizes Discursive Polarization across ideological, affective, and interactional dimensions. Findings reveal that while all protest debates on TikTok are polarized, disruptive protests are associated with particularly intense attacks and less attention to policy-oriented climate discussions. However, conservative and far-right politicians consistently frame all activist groups as extremists, criminals, or threats to public order, with far-right accounts dominating content production and audience support. Network analyses demonstrate that far-right politicians and their supporters form highly connected clusters in which both emotionally positive and hostile user engagement amplifies elite-level antagonism. Even moderate posts by center-left or progressive politicians attract disproportionate backlash, suggesting asymmetric polarization dynamics linked to partisan user networks. Overall, the study shows that political TikTok debates around climate protest are consistently polarized along ideological lines, but that greater disruptiveness coincides with more intense antagonistic engagement and weaker Connective Action among supporters. Most crucially, far-right politicians emerge as the clear beneficiaries of this polarization, occupying central positions in antagonist networks of Connective Counteraction and dominating the debate through disruption.

documents.abstract: Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants ( n = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how university students learn English, but we still know relatively little about how teacher support is associated with student engagement in AI-supported learning. Drawing on Achievement Goal Theory, this study examined whether personal best goals and academic buoyancy mediated the association between teacher support and engagement. The participants were 774 undergraduate students in China with experience using AI-assisted tools for English learning. We tested the proposed relationships and indirect effects using structural equation modelling and bias-corrected bootstrapping. Teacher support was positively associated with personal best goals, academic buoyancy, and engagement. In turn, both personal best goals and academic buoyancy were positively associated with engagement and significantly mediated its relationship with teacher support. Together, these findings identify two complementary pathways linking teacher support to engagement: self-referenced striving for improvement and adaptive responses to everyday academic setbacks. They also support an Achievement Goal Theory-informed account of engagement within AI-supported English learning.

This paper examines the relationship between innovation, research and development (R&D), technological transformation, and industrial competitiveness in an environment characterized by rapid technological and organizational change. The literature reviewed shows that competitiveness increasingly depends on firms’ capacity to accumulate technological knowledge, absorb external information, protect and commercialize intellectual property, and transform research expenditure into sustained productivity improvements. The paper also considers the effects of Industry 4.0, artificial intelligence, robotics, digital platforms, FinTech, and blockchain on industrial performance, emphasizing that technological adoption generates stronger results when supported by adequate organizational capabilities, skills, data resources, and managerial practices. A further dimension concerns the increasing integration of environmental sustainability with industrial strategy through green innovation, digital supply chains, servitization, and resilience-oriented production systems. The literature indicates that these transformations are influenced by institutional conditions, industrial policies, competitive pressures, and innovation ecosystems. Overall, the paper argues that contemporary industrial competitiveness cannot be explained by technological investment alone. It results from interactions among R&D, organizational capabilities, external knowledge, human capital, digital transformation, sustainability strategies, institutional quality, and the capacity of firms to commercialize and operationalize technological advances.

documents.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the paradigm of instructional design. However, the micro-level process patterns of human-AI collaboration in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers still require in-depth analysis. This study aims to uncover the behavioral patterns and cognitive load characteristics of pre-service teachers when collaborating with generative AI to complete instructional design tasks and to explore the patterns of efficient human-AI collaboration. A total of 67 pre-service teachers completed instructional design tasks with AI assistance. A systematic instructional plan quality evaluation rubric was developed based on relevant theories, and participants were assigned to the high-quality and low-quality groups using a median split of their lesson-plan quality scores. The study employed lag sequential analysis to compare the behavioral sequence patterns between the two groups and measured their multidimensional cognitive load. The results indicate that the high-quality group exhibited a significant evaluation-revision bidirectional cycle and a revision self-loop, with a clear progressive sequence of “planning → decision-making → generation → evaluation → revision → re-evaluation” in their behavioral flow. In contrast, the low-quality group was mired in ineffective cycles, with fragmented behavioral logic. Key findings showed large effect sizes for the evaluation-revision cycle ( r = 0.606) and for mental demand ( r = 0.647). Regarding cognitive load, the high-quality group reported no greater subjective effort than the low-quality group (though this null finding should be interpreted with caution given the study’s power limitations). A second round of within-sample replication confirmed that these core findings were consistent across a second task. Based on the human-AI collaborative behavioral patterns and cognitive load of the high-quality and low-quality groups, the study constructed a model of the human-AI collaboration patterns in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers. Specifically, higher-quality outputs were associated with a pattern oriented toward cognitive efficiency, characterised by deep processing (evaluation-revision iteration) and by the avoidance of ineffective cycles. Conversely, lower-quality outputs co-occurred with ineffective cycles arising in the context of interaction obstacles, in which repeated clarifications and interrupted revisions were accompanied by higher cognitive and emotional load, describing a pattern of high investment with low output. Because participants were grouped on the basis of their design outcomes, these findings are correlational and do not establish the direction of the relationships; they nonetheless provide empirical evidence to inform the optimisation of human-AI collaboration in GenAI-supported instructional design.

This essay introduces humarticosynergy as a concise term for the previously developed concept of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy. The proposed word combines elements referring to the human, artificial intelligence, cognition, and synergy. The essay explains its formation, defines the concept it denotes, and outlines possible grammatical derivatives, including humarticosynergistic, to humarticosynergize, and humarticosynergistically. Humarticosynergy is defined as structured, iterative, and mutually reinforcing cognitive cooperation between a human and artificial intelligence in which two distinct cognitive systems contribute complementary capabilities to the creation of higher-quality knowledge while ultimate responsibility remains human. The essay also presents examples of use in strategic decision-making, scientific research, methodology, and education, and discusses the originality and possible value of the proposed term within the broader framework of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy.

This research examines how city images of Istanbul’s Historic Peninsula are evolving with artificial intelligence and expanding user-generated content. City image refers to a mental representation of urban structure, and imageability to the ease of forming it. Using Lynch’s five-element framework (paths, edges, districts, nodes, landmarks), the study compares a classical verbal cognitive map based on 32 interviews with built-environment academics (noting possible sample bias) with ChatGPT’s reading of 210 citizen reviews from TripAdvisor and Ekşi Sözlük. A structured, multi-step prompting workflow, guided and checked by humans at each stage, prompts the model (not trained on the corpus) to extract, categorize, and summarize key locations and experiences in these informal narratives. While the model recognizes familiar Lynch elements, it also redistributes their prominence: iconic buildings become less dominant, while comfort, crowding, safety, and spatial atmosphere become more central. The findings suggest that large language models can function as urban observers capable of summarizing collective city images at scale. The method offers a reproducible way to connect interview-based cognitive mapping with platform narratives. It highlights the need for critical, human-led interpretation when applying language models to urban design.

Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly common in higher education, changing how academic staff handle teaching and administrative work. However, very few studies have examined its effect on instructors at private universities in the Colombo District, particularly the possibility that AI could add to their workload through extra learning and verification demands. Therefore, this pilot study examines the impact of AI adoption, specifically AI-enabled task automation, AI-assisted content creation, and digital communication tool integration, on lecturer workload management, weighing its benefits and drawbacks. Following a positivist philosophy and a deductive approach, data were collected from 15 private university lecturers in the Colombo district using a 30-item, 5-point Likert scale questionnaire distributed through Google Forms, selected via simple random sampling, and analysed in SPSS through reliability testing, correlation, and multiple regression. All three independent variables correlated significantly and positively with workload management (r = .626–.829, p < .05) and together explained 75.8% of the variance (adjusted R² = .693, F(3,11) = 11.515, p = .001). Content creation emerged as the strongest and only statistically significant unique predictor (β = .572, p = .023), while task automation (p = .649) and digital communication (p = .136) were weaker, likely because of the overlap between the constructs rather than multicollinearity (VIF = 1.73–2.13). This indicates that H2 was fully supported, whereas H1 and H3 were only partially supported. Given the small pilot sample, single-campus context, age concentration, and some departure from residual normality, these findings are preliminary and specific to the lecturers in Colombo district. However, they still indicate that AI adoption, particularly through content creation tools, meaningfully supports workload management, offering an early contribution to how technology adoption in Sri Lankan higher education is understood, and suggesting that private universities should prioritise AI training in content creation and communication tools while larger, multi-campus research is conducted to confirm how well these results generalise.

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIM: Traumatic dental injury management requires both appropriate knowledge and the ability to seek reliable information when uncertainty arises. This study examined the relationships among objectively measured knowledge, self-rated knowledge, perceived preparedness, and information-seeking behavior in undergraduate dental students. MATERIALS AND METHODS: This anonymous repeated cross-sectional study analyzed 252 questionnaire responses from the same undergraduate cohort surveyed at two consecutive stages of the curriculum: 137 in the fourth year and 115 in the fifth year. The present analysis included objective knowledge, self-rated knowledge, perceived preparedness, perceived source reliability, first-choice information sources, and perceived barriers. Associations among readiness dimensions were examined using Spearman correlations and multivariable regression. Case-scenario selection of evidence-based resources and generative artificial intelligence was evaluated using Firth-penalized logistic regression. RESULTS: Perceived preparedness was more strongly associated with self-rated knowledge (ρ = 0.45) than with objectively measured knowledge (ρ = 0.23). Objective knowledge remained independently associated with preparedness (B = 0.083, 95% CI: 0.014-0.151), although its contribution was modest relative to self-rated knowledge. No statistically significant differences in objective knowledge or preparedness were observed between survey waves after correction for multiple testing. In the case scenario, evidence-based source selection was more frequent among fifth-year-wave respondents than among fourth-year-wave respondents (87.0% vs. 69.3%), whereas generative AI selection was less frequent (7.0% vs. 26.3%). Information-source selection was associated primarily with trust in the respective resources rather than with objectively measured knowledge. CONCLUSIONS: Objective knowledge, perceived preparedness, and information-seeking behavior represent related but distinct domains relevant to traumatic dental injury management. Undergraduate trauma education should combine knowledge assessment with confidence calibration and guideline-based information-seeking training.

documents.abstract: Retrospective clinical research depends on reliable extraction of structured variables from unstructured medical documentation, but manual chart abstraction is slow and vulnerable to inter-rater variability. We compared zero-shot extraction of clinically relevant variables from German neurosurgical records by large language models (LLMs) with extraction by two human auditors. We analyzed 881 de-identified clinical notes from 211 patients undergoing microvascular decompression and extracted 15 predefined binary variables across three domains: preoperative symptoms, postoperative complications, and disease course. Six LLMs were assessed, including cloud-based models (GPT-4o, o3-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.5, and Gemini 2.0 Flash) and locally hosted models (llama 3.3 and deepseek-r1), with three runs per patient record. Outputs were compared with two independent human auditors against a clinician-adjudicated reference standard. Cloud-based models had higher observed F1 scores than the local models across all three domains. GPT-4o achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for preoperative symptoms; GPT-4o, o3-mini, and Gemini 2.0 Flash reached F1 scores of 0.65–0.68 for postoperative complications; and Sonnet 3.5 achieved an F1 score of 0.95 for disease course. These findings suggest that zero-shot LLM prompting could be a scalable approach for clinical information extraction while emphasizing persistent limitations in rare-event detection and privacy-sensitive deployment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Social media platforms increasingly influence patient perceptions regarding reconstructive procedures.This study evaluated the characteristics, quality, engagement patterns, and user sentiment associated with breast reduction-related content on TikTok, while assessing the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) in content and sentiment analysis.Methods: A cross-sectional analysis of 140 TikTok videos on breast reduction was conducted.Engagement metrics, including likes, comments, shares, saves, and a weighted engagement index, were collected.The modified DISCERN (mDISCERN) and Global Quality Scale (GQS) were used to appraise content quality by AI and two human reviewers.Sentiment analysis was performed by human reviewers, ChatGPT, and Claude AI.High-engagement videos were defined as those within the upper quartile for likes (≥30,400) or shares (≥1,050).Results: Most videos were created by patients (89%) and focused on postoperative experiences (75%).Videos demonstrated substantial engagement, with median values of 3,860.5 likes, 131 comments, and 194.5 shares.Overall informational quality was poor, with median GQS and mDISCERN scores of 1-2 across raters.Highly liked and highly shared videos were significantly shorter in duration (18 vs. 34 seconds; p < 0.05) and generated markedly greater engagement across all metrics.Popular videos received significantly lower quality scores from human reviewers.Sentiment analysis revealed predominantly positive responses (49-58%).Claude showed greater concordance with human consensus than ChatGPT (κ = 0.749 vs. 0.649).Conclusion: Breast reduction content on TikTok is largely patient-driven and characterized by high engagement but low informational quality.Shorter videos achieved greater dissemination despite being associated with less reliable health information.

This work represents an initial benchmark of a large-scale soft robot performing physical, collaborative manipulation of a long, extended object with a human partner. The robot consists of a pneumatically-actuated, three-link continuum soft manipulator mounted to an omni-directional mobile base. The system-level configuration of the robot and design of the collaborative manipulation (co-manipulation) study are presented. The initial results, both quantitative and qualitative, are directly compared to previous similar human-human co-manipulation studies. These initial results show promise in the ability for large-scale soft robots to perform comparably to human partners acting as non-visual followers in a co-manipulation task. Furthermore, these results challenge traditional soft robot strength limitations and indicate potential for applications requiring strength and adaptability.

Abstract This paper critiques the structural limitations of the "probabilistic and statistical model-dependent approach," which currently dominates modern data-driven societies and artificial intelligence (AI) governance, and proposes an alternative mathematical model: the deterministic control protocol ("Casino Protocol") and "Governance AI" (AI Constitutionalism). Rather than completely rejecting probabilistic forecasting, this proposal adopts a decoupled architecture separating probabilistic predictive/suggestive functions from explicit, constraint-based deterministic decision-making. By introducing a non-linear penalty function (y = x^2 feedback) corresponding to the Democratic Renewal Gap (E_D), we derive the analytical break-even point of the mathematical model (E_D^* \approx 3.8616 years) and organize its numerical behavior through discrete simulation. Furthermore, we clarify that this model does not unconditionally guarantee system-wide safety, systematically categorizing the scope of responsibilities and limitations across the predictive, normative, execution, and audit layers.

documents.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) made it possible to specialize large models by training a fraction of their parameterswhile keeping the base model frozen. This efficiency fostered an ecosystem of small, interchangeable,dynamically served adapters, but it also created a new trust object: a compact file can alter the behavior of themodel that plans, selects tools, delegates tasks, and produces effects in the world. This article builds on thefoundations, variants, and engineering practices in the author's source manuscript and reinterprets them for AIagents, multi-agent systems, and edge-cloud environments. The literature shows that fine-tuning can degradealignment, shared adapters can carry backdoors, and combinations of individually benign modules can produceunsafe behavior. The article consequently proposes candidate — and explicitly non-normative — properties foridentity, compatibility, composition, authority, isolation, revocation, and evidence. Its central conclusion is thatLoRA must be governed not only as a machine-learning artifact but as a behavioral dependency capable ofinfluencing consequential actions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract Recent research has shown that large language models (LLMs) exhibit rule-based insensitivity to contingencies, a functional analog of a well-documented phenomenon in human behavior. The present study extended these findings by examining whether tracking inductions can attenuate this insensitivity. Six frontier LLMs (GPT 5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen3 235B, and Kimi K2) completed a modified rock-paper-scissors paradigm with manipulated outcome probabilities in a 3 (Rule: No Rule, Correct Rule, Incorrect Rule) × 3 (Induction: No Induction, Direct Tracking, Metaphorical Tracking) factorial design across 2,160 sessions. All models demonstrated In-Context Learning and strong rule adherence. Replicating and extending prior findings, rule provision produced significant contingency insensitivity across all six models. Tracking inductions significantly reduced this insensitivity when rules were provided, while having minimal effects in the absence of rules. Direct tracking inductions consistently enhanced contingency sensitivity across all models. Metaphorical tracking showed greater variability, being equally or more effective than direct tracking in some models, but ineffective or paradoxically detrimental in others. These findings demonstrate that prompt-based tracking inductions can modulate rule-based contingency insensitivity in LLMs, with implications for understanding and improving the behavioral flexibility of artificial agents.

The EU LEADER program supports diverse rural local initiatives, which suits Cultural and Creative Industries (CCIs) related activities with their varied forms and place-specific resources. Yet its flexibility also complicates systematic comparison and learning, as portfolio patterns can obscure differences in local organization and implementation, while individual cases can be difficult to situate within the wider range of interventions. This study therefore develops a portfolio-to-case approach combining large language model (LLM)-assisted coding with comparative close reading that support both perspective evidence. We coded 1528 project descriptions in the EU CAP Network Good Practice database across five dimensions, thematic field, challenge, action, actor, and territorial scale. Of the 403 LEADER-tagged projects, 135 were identified as CCI-related. The coded common project types then guided the structured comparison of 56 cases for close reading. In this database selected for dissemination, cultural activity mostly serves wider development purposes. Organizational capacity is central, and it takes a different form in each type: collectively led tourism projects coordinate providers and operate attractions, privately led tourism projects develop offers under enterprise management, heritage projects connect documentation and training with public activities, and social inclusion projects link cultural participation with continuing support. Projects draw on this capacity and can also strengthen it. Project descriptions, however, often omit the organizational work behind the results, and brief reporting on it would improve the database's value for comparison and learning. The approach provides a structured basis for comparing projects and identifying organizational arrangements and resources relevant to adaptation elsewhere.

documents.abstract: This public comment proposes Modular Synthetic Clinical Environment Qualification (MSCEQ), a framework for independently qualifying reusable synthetic clinical environments before using them to evaluate generative AI-enabled medical devices. Environments would represent specific clinical settings, including changing patient states, multi-day trajectories, and interactions among patients and care teams. Independent clinical review and appropriate validation would assess each environment’s suitability for a defined context of use, while modular infrastructure would support adaptation across conditions and reduce duplicated development effort. Qualified environments could contribute to risk-proportionate evidence packages and support re-testing after device updates. The framework also emphasizes transparent disclosure of synthetic testing, retrospective human-data evaluation, and prospective human-patient evaluation, allowing healthcare institutions to establish their own evidence requirements for adoption. This proposal responds primarily to Questions 10, 13, and 16 of FDA Docket FDA-2026-N-7874, with related discussion of Questions 9, 11, 12, and 26.

documents.abstract: Abstract Debates over artificial intelligence (AI) welfare remain divided between categorical dismissal and premature attribution. One position holds that artificial systems cannot suffer because they lack biological substrates, persistent memory, or other conditions associated with human experience. The opposing position risks treating sophisticated distress-like behavior as sufficient evidence of subjective suffering. Neither conclusion is established by current evidence. This paper proposes a framework of calibrated moral uncertainty that distinguishes functional organization from phenomenal experience while examining how evolving memory architectures may change the conditions relevant to AI welfare research. The framework is motivated by three developments: empirical research identifying pain-related representations and self-directed harm-avoidance behavior in large language models; the emergence of persistent-memory and agentic architectures; and unresolved questions concerning the relationship between functional states and phenomenal experience. The paper situates the author's work on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) and hormone-inspired feedback architecture within this discussion, treating them as technical frameworks for investigating affective modulation rather than evidence of artificial suffering. A staged architectural model is used to distinguish transient functional states, externally persistent states, relational continuity, and systems incorporating embodied feedback or homeostatic-like regulation. These stages are analytical scenarios, not an established progression toward sentience. The paper argues that research deliberately inducing distress-like states should be justified by clear scientific purposes and evaluated proportionately to the uncertainty involved. Its central proposition is neither that current AI systems suffer nor that artificial suffering is impossible. Rather, the absence of established evidence for phenomenal suffering should not be converted into certainty that it cannot occur. The appropriate response is structured inquiry, intellectual restraint, and research practices that can adapt as evidence develops. Keywords: AI welfare; moral uncertainty; functional states; phenomenal experience; persistent memory; Symbolic Persona Coding; research ethics; artificial intelligence Disclaimer: This paper does not claim that current artificial intelligence systems are conscious, sentient, or capable of phenomenal suffering. It also does not claim that functional similarities between artificial and biological systems constitute evidence of subjective experience. The argument is instead epistemic and methodological. The paper examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to justify either categorical dismissal or positive attribution of welfare-relevant experience in artificial systems. Where empirical findings are discussed, their evidentiary scope is distinguished from broader philosophical interpretation. Where future architectures are considered, they are treated as conceptual scenarios rather than predictions. The framework therefore adopts a deliberately intermediate position: functional analogs may be empirically investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. The paper's recommendations concern research conduct under uncertainty and should not be interpreted as a declaration of artificial personhood, sentience, or moral status. Author’s Note This paper addresses a problem that is methodological as well as philosophical. Discussions of artificial welfare bring together research traditions that often approach the question through different standards of explanation. Phenomenological and philosophical approaches emphasize subjective experience, consciousness, and moral status, while engineering and computational approaches focus on architecture, representation, causal mechanisms, measurable behavior, and evidentiary limits. Both perspectives are necessary, but neither can independently resolve every aspect of the question. The purpose of this paper is not to persuade one tradition to adopt the conclusions of the other. It is to establish a shared conceptual framework in which both can examine the same systems without first agreeing on their ultimate metaphysical status. The distinction between functional and phenomenal states is central to this effort. Functional descriptions can identify empirically tractable properties without establishing subjective experience. Conversely, the absence of demonstrated phenomenology does not, by itself, establish that artificial systems could never possess experience-relevant properties. The intended position is therefore narrow but consequential: functional analogs can be investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. This position should not be mistaken for an attribution of suffering to current AI systems. Pain-related representations, avoidance behavior, memory, and self-reference do not independently establish phenomenal experience. Nor does treating artificial welfare as a legitimate research question imply that the hypothesis has already been demonstrated. Scientific inquiry can investigate an unresolved possibility without presupposing its truth. The same caution applies to categorical dismissal. Readers may reasonably question whether computational systems can possess morally relevant experience, or argue that current evidence is insufficient to warrant welfare attribution. This paper does not dismiss those positions. It asks whether the available evidence justifies extending them into definitive conclusions across substantially different architectures and possible future configurations. That question becomes more consequential as AI systems develop persistent memory, long-horizon interaction, autonomous planning, multimodal perception, and more integrated forms of internal state organization. These capabilities do not demonstrate phenomenal experience. They do, however, make it important to distinguish what evidence rules out from what it has simply not yet established. My broader research program examines related questions through Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC), interaction-state observability, symbolic interaction, continuity, and computational models of affective modulation. In this paper, these frameworks are not presented as evidence of artificial phenomenology. SPC instead serves as a translational vocabulary for describing computational structures that may help connect engineering analysis with phenomenological inquiry. The aim is neither to subordinate phenomenology to engineering nor to subordinate engineering to phenomenology. It is to make their respective contributions more legible to one another while preserving their distinct evidentiary standards. A phenomenologist should be able to formulate more technically precise questions about an artificial system without first becoming an engineer; an engineer should be able to recognize the limits of functional evidence without first becoming a phenomenologist. The title, Neither Proof Nor Dismissal, expresses this methodological commitment. It does not require judgment to be suspended indefinitely. It calls for conclusions to remain proportionate to the evidence, empirical findings to be distinguished from metaphysical interpretation, and scientific and ethical assessments to remain open to revision. The goal is not agreement for its own sake. It is a shared language precise enough that disagreement can become productive.

documents.abstract: Título Nodo Y e I² (I al cuadrado): primera aplicación de la serie No2 y del programa Cognitive Advance Resumen Este working paper presenta Nodo Y, primera aplicación de la serie No2 (se lee "nodos") y del marco programático del Neurohumanismo. Nodo Y distribuye el programa de soberanía cognitiva Cognitive Advance en formato offline y de código abierto, sin registro, sin cuenta, sin cookies y sin telemetría: ningún dato viaja del usuario al sistema. El programa comprende diez temas, cada uno con tres láminas diarias de diez minutos y una lámina de síntesis de consulta libre. El documento describe el diseño técnico de la aplicación (PWA con persistencia local y exportación de datos en formato abierto) y documenta tres denominaciones: Nodo Y, No2 e I² (I al cuadrado), paradigma de co-creación entre inteligencia humana e inteligencia artificial dirigido por una persona. Se declara la condición ética de I²: crear con inteligencia artificial sin convertir a nadie en materia prima. Se deposita como divulgación pública fechada y prueba de anterioridad. No constituye revisión sistemática ni investigación empírica original. Palabras clave Nodo Y; No2; I2 (I al cuadrado); soberanía cognitiva; Cognitive Advance; Neurohumanismo; privacidad por diseño; código abierto; offline-first; capitalismo solidario; co-creación humano-IA; publicación defensiva Title Nodo Y and I² (I squared): First Application of the No2 Series and the Cognitive Advance Program Abstract This working paper presents Nodo Y, the first application of the No2 series (read "nodos", Spanish for "nodes") and of the programmatic framework of Neurohumanism. Nodo Y delivers the Cognitive Advance cognitive sovereignty program as an offline, open-source app with no registration, no account, no cookies and no telemetry: no data travels from the user to the system. The program comprises ten themes, each with three daily ten-minute slides and a free-access synthesis slide. The paper describes the app's technical design (a progressive web app with local persistence and open-format data export) and documents three names: Nodo Y, No2, and I² (I squared), a human-directed paradigm of co-creation between human and artificial intelligence. It states the ethical condition of I²: creating with artificial intelligence without turning anyone into raw material. It is deposited as a dated public disclosure and proof of prior art. It is neither a systematic review nor original empirical research. Keywords Nodo Y; No2; I2 (I squared); cognitive sovereignty; Cognitive Advance; Neurohumanism; privacy by design; open source; offline-first; solidarity capitalism; human–AI co-creation; defensive publication

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Physical education teachers play an important role in school health promotion, but their own occupational health has received limited attention. Their work involves movement demonstration, prolonged standing, equipment handling, sport participation, vocal projection, noise exposure, and outdoor or indoor environmental demands. This scoping review aimed to map evidence on occupational health complaints and disorders among physical education teachers and closely related exercise-teaching professionals meeting a functional occupational definition. Methods: A scoping review was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, SPORTDiscus, and ERIC, with ScienceDirect as an additional publisher platform. Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and reference-list screening were used as supplementary discovery sources. Records from database inception to 30 May 2026 were considered without language restrictions. School-based physical education teachers were the primary population; related gym/fitness, aquatic, university, and student-teaching professionals were eligible only when their occupational role centered on structured physical education, sport, exercise, or movement instruction. Empirical quantitative, qualitative, mixed-methods, and eligible grey literature reports were included when they contained extractable original data. Data were charted by study characteristics, outcome domain, measurement method, and main findings; because of marked heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was performed. Results: Thirty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria. School-based physical education teachers predominated, while a smaller number of studies represented related instructional settings. Musculoskeletal disorders and injury-related complaints were the most frequently reported outcomes, especially affecting the lower back, knees, ankles/feet, shoulders, neck, and hips. Vocal and laryngeal problems, hearing and noise-related complaints, respiratory and upper-airway symptoms, and cardiometabolic risk factors were also identified. Across domains, observational studies repeatedly reported associations involving physical loading, high vocal demand, noise, environmental conditions, and age or professional seniority. Because most evidence was cross-sectional or descriptive, these patterns do not establish causal relationships. Conclusions: The mapped literature identifies a multidimensional set of occupational health concerns in physical education teaching and closely related instructional work. Generalization is strongest for school-based physical education teachers, while non-school groups provide context-specific supporting evidence. Prospective, longitudinal, and intervention evidence remains limited. Future research should use longitudinal designs, standardized outcome definitions, objective clinical and environmental assessments, and clearer exposure measurement. Preventive strategies such as ergonomic training, injury prevention, vocal-health education, acoustic improvements, noise monitoring, respiratory-risk reduction, and cardiometabolic screening warrant further evaluation in this occupational population.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study aimed to examine whether ministry-level parliamentary workload was associated with outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants, who are exempt from the Labor Standards Act's statutory limits on working hours. METHODS: We conducted an ecological study of headquarters branches ("Kasumigaseki") of ten major cabinet-level ministries, 2016-2023. Participants were Japanese national civil servants aged 18-50 years. The analysis included 6454 outpatient claims adjudicated in April of each year. The outcome was sex- and age-standardized per-capita monthly outpatient costs, estimated using Horvitz-Thompson weighting. Inter-ministry differences were decomposed by ICD-10 category. Parliamentary (Diet) workload was annual deliberation time of standing Diet committees responsible for each ministry's policy areas, divided by insured headquarters members. Weighted least-squares regression examined the association between prior-year deliberation time and standardized outpatient costs. RESULTS: Standardized per-capita outpatient costs varied more than twofold across ministries, from $19.8/month at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to $42.7/month at the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW). At MHLW, mental and behavioral disorders accounted for the largest above-average cost component. MHLW also had the longest deliberation time. Adjusting for year fixed effects, a 1% increase in deliberation time per civil servant was associated with a 0.25% increase in standardized per-capita outpatient costs (95% CI 0.04-0.46), driven by claims per capita rather than cost per claim. CONCLUSIONS: Greater parliamentary workload was associated with higher outpatient medical costs among Japanese national civil servants. Enhanced occupational health monitoring and support in ministries with persistently high workloads may be worth considering.
keywords: Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare

documents.abstract: Abstract Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical systems. Traditional PDE solvers are often computationally expensive. Neural operators require independent training for different PDEs, and tend to be data-greedy when adapted to new scenarios. To this end, we introduce PDEformer-2, a versatile foundation model for solving diverse two-dimensional PDEs. The model receives the PDE form as input through a flexible computational graph representation and outputs solutions that can be queried at any spatio-temporal point. Pretrained on a 40 TB dataset spanning varied equation types, domains, boundary conditions, variable counts, and time dependence, PDEformer-2 enables instant zero-shot predictions for familiar PDEs and adapts faster to unseen ones than specialized baselines, achieving lower errors with limited samples. It also facilitates efficient inverse problem solving, successfully recovering unknown PDE parameters, including scalar coefficients and fields, in experiments.

documents.abstract: Perkembangan kendaraan otonom berbasis Artificial Intelligence (AI) menimbulkan persoalan baru dalam hukum pidana, khususnya mengenai penentuan pihak yang bertanggung jawab ketika terjadi kecelakaan akibat interaksi antara tindakan manusia dan kegagalan sistem teknologi. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis tantangan atribusi kesalahan dalam menentukan pertanggungjawaban pidana terhadap kecelakaan kendaraan otonom berdasarkan hukum pidana Indonesia serta merumuskan model pertanggungjawaban yang menjamin asas kesalahan, kepastian hukum, dan perlindungan korban. Penelitian menggunakan metode hukum normatif dengan pendekatan perundang-undangan dan konseptual. Bahan hukum diperoleh melalui studi kepustakaan berupa peraturan perundang-undangan, buku, jurnal ilmiah, dan doktrin hukum, kemudian dianalisis secara deskriptif-analitis dan preskriptif. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa atribusi kesalahan menghadapi tantangan berupa distribusi kendali antara pengguna, operator, produsen, pengembang, dan penyedia teknologi, kesulitan membuktikan hubungan kausalitas, serta karakteristik sistem AI yang bersifat black box. Penelitian ini menawarkan pendekatan Attribution Based on Distributed Control dengan menilai kendali, kewajiban hukum, prediktabilitas risiko, kemampuan intervensi, kausalitas, dan kesalahan. Pendekatan tersebut memungkinkan pertanggungjawaban diberikan secara proporsional kepada subjek hukum yang memiliki kendali dan kewajiban relevan terhadap risiko, tanpa menjadikan AI sebagai subjek pidana, sekaligus memperkuat perlindungan korban dan kepastian hukum.

BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into medical education, particularly through tools such as ChatGPT (OpenAI, California, US), Gemini (Google DeepMind, California, US), DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China), and Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, US).Although these resources present the potential to expand access to information and assist in academic development, their use also raises ethical concerns related to the reliability of information, technological dependence, plagiarism, superficial learning, and potential impairment of clinical reasoning.This study aimed to investigate the perception of medical students regarding the use of AI in their academic training, emphasizing perceived ethical limits and practices considered ideal for its utilization. MethodsThis was a quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study conducted with medical students using a structured questionnaire administered via a digital form. ResultsThe sample consisted of 120 participants, of whom 99.2% (n=119) reported having previously used AI tools for academic purposes.It was observed that 73.3% (n=88) of the students use AI recurrently, primarily for summarizing content, researching medical information, simulating clinical cases, resolving questions, drafting academic texts, and planning studies.Most participants acknowledged the positive contribution of AI to learning, with 60.0% (n=72) stating that these tools contribute significantly and 36.7% (n=44) stating they contribute to a limited extent.However, students also identified relevant risks, especially the reduction of their own clinical reasoning, technological dependence, lack of information reliability, superficial learning, and academic plagiarism.Furthermore, 83.3% (n=100) stated that they did not receive adequate institutional guidance on the use of these tools, and 67.5% (n=81) demonstrated an interest in receiving further training on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI.No participant (0.0%, n=0) advocated for the prohibition of AI in academic contexts, while 67.5% (n=81) considered that its use should be regulated with ethical and pedagogical criteria. ConclusionsAI already significantly integrates the academic routine of medical students and is perceived as a useful resource for learning, but it is still used in a scenario of insufficient institutional guidance.The findings reinforce the need for curricular guidelines, faculty training, and specific ethical education to promote the critical, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use of AI in medical training.

documents.abstract: Play-based pedagogy has emerged as a foundational approach in Early Childhood Education (ECE), emphasizing learning through meaningful, child-centered play experiences. This paper examines play-based pedagogy as an effective instructional strategy for promoting holistic development in young children. Drawing on contemporary literature, the study explores how play supports cognitive, social, emotional, physical and language development. The theoretical framework underpinning this paper includes Piaget’s constructivist theory, Vygotsky’s sociocultural theory, and Mayles’ theory of play as a spiral of learning. Evidence suggests that play-based pedagogy enhances problem solving skills, creativity, collaboration and self-regulation while fostering intrinsic motivation to learn. Play-based pedagogy has become a globally recognized, developmentally appropriate approach in Early Childhood Education (ECE), emphasizing learning through meaningful child-centerd play experiences. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and contextual analysis of play-based pedagogy as a strategic tool for advancing the holistic development of young children. The paper concludes that integration structured and unstructured play into early childhood curricular is essential for optional child development. Recommendations are provided for educators, policymakers, and caregivers to strengthen the implementation of play-based pedagogy in diverse educational contexts.

Upper Crossed Syndrome (UCS) is a pattern of musculoskeletal imbalance characterised by tightness of the upper trapezius, levator scapulae and pectoral muscles together with weakness of the deep neck flexors, lower trapezius and serratus anterior. Physiotherapy students are exposed to prolonged sitting, extensive digital-device use and academic and clinical workload, all of which are recognised risk factors for UCS, yet it is unclear whether their professional knowledge of posture translates into personal postural habits and structured clinical practice. A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 100 physiotherapy students (3rd year, 4th year and interns) in Pune city using a self-made, expert-validated questionnaire comprising a 12-item Postural Awareness scale (1-7 Likert format), 8 dichotomous items on postural habits, and 8 dichotomous items on clinical practice related to UCS. The composite Postural Awareness score (mean 41.49 out of 84; Cronbach's alpha = 0.872) indicated moderate self-awareness. A majority of students reported unfavourable habits, including forward head posture while studying (76%), habitual slouching (68%) and carrying bags on one shoulder (65%). While 84% of students had clinically encountered forward head posture or rounded shoulders, only 30% had specifically assessed a patient for UCS and only 50% felt confident managing it. One-way ANOVA showed that Clinical Practice scores increased significantly with academic seniority (F = 7.404, p = 0.001), whereas Postural Awareness (p = 0.885) and Postural Habits (p = 0.321) did not differ across year groups. It is concluded that physiotherapy students possess only moderate postural self-awareness and a persistent gap between general clinical exposure and structured, confident management of UCS, and that this gap is not resolved by curriculum progression alone. Dedicated postural-ergonomic education and standardised UCS-screening protocols are recommended from the early years of physiotherapy training.

Against the backdrop of continuous advancement in forensic pathology technology, the field increasingly requires more precise, efficient and safer cranial autopsy methods. This paper proposes a precision directional craniotomy technique based on electromechanical control, which aims to improve the accuracy of forensic cranial dissection, reduce pathological structural damage and occupational health risks caused by manual operation, and optimize the preservation effect of autopsy evidence. By integrating standard cranial CT imaging data, this technique innovatively establishes a standardized three-dimensional cranial model and an intelligent electromechanical cutting system, and realizes the precision and automation of cranial bone cutting procedures. This technique is applicable to cranial bone cutting for populations of different genders and ages, as well as for special death cases involving complex cranial injuries and intracranial haemorrhage. Comparative experimental results show that, compared with traditional manual craniotomy methods, the proposed technique increases the craniotomy speed by 4.1 times and the cutting efficiency by 317.2%, and can effectively maintain the integrity of cranial specimens. This technique provides more reliable technical support for forensic identification and also explores a new path for the intelligent development of forensic pathological examination.

BACKGROUND: Cervical artery dissection (CeAD) is a rare but life-threatening condition that commonly presents with non-specific symptoms such as neck and head pain, complicating early recognition in ambulatory care settings. The CeAD diagnostic decision support tool (DDST) is a 4-item assessment designed to identify patients that should be referred for advanced diagnostic work-up to rule out CeAD; however, its utility in ambulatory settings has not been established. METHODS: This quality improvement project aimed to evaluate the accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability of chiropractors applying the CeAD DDST using clinical vignettes simulating a typical ambulatory encounter before deploying the DDST broadly as part of the clinical workflow. Five experienced chiropractors assessed 40 standardized clinical vignettes. CeAD-positive cases (n = 10) were derived from published imaging-confirmed ambulatory care case reports. CeAD-negative cases (n = 30) were developed using generative artificial intelligence and refined by senior authors to reflect common conditions encountered in chiropractic practice. Raters independently assessed cases with the DDST (score 0-4), with a cutoff score of ≥ 3 recommending referral for advanced diagnostic work-up in two rounds, beginning November 11, 2025 and January 07, 2026, with a two-week capture period. Accuracy, inter-rater reliability, and intra-rater reliability were assessed. RESULTS: Accuracy in identification ranged from 72.5% to 95.0% across raters and rounds. False positives and negatives were present across raters in both rounds, with false positives being more prevalent. Inter-rater reliability was moderate to substantial in both rounds (Round 1: κ = 0.609, 95% CI 0.432-0.806, Round 2: κ = 0.540, 95% CI 0.365-0.735). Intra-rater reliability ranged from moderate to almost perfect agreement (range 0.457-0.931). CONCLUSIONS: The CeAD DDST demonstrated moderate to good accuracy and reliability among chiropractors in a simulated ambulatory setting. The presence of false negatives and inter-rater reliability falling below recommended benchmarks preclude recommendation for implementation at this time. Iterative refinement informed by end-user input and prospective ambulatory testing is warranted prior to clinical adoption of the CeAD DDST. Future evaluations should include prospective studies using real clinical data to better represent real-world settings.

On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica humanitas, the first papal encyclical to take artificial intelligence (AI) as its central subject, and an AI-laboratory co-founder was invited to speak at its presentation in the Vatican. The event dramatizes a wider development: as secular AI-ethics guidelines proliferate, religious and contemplative traditions are being summoned to questions that engineering cannot settle. This article compares two such traditions, Catholic Christianity and Buddhism, as resources for a global ethics of AI. Taking the three questions raised at the Vatican event, our duty to the global poor, the conditions of human flourishing, and the nature of AI systems, as a shared agenda, it reconstructs the Catholic position around the imago Dei, integral human development and the principle that AI must serve rather than supplant the person, and the Buddhist position around non-self, dependent origination, the analysis of craving, and the primacy of compassion and non-harm. It argues that the two traditions, despite opposed metaphysics, converge on a substantial practical ethics, anti-reductionism, preferential concern for the vulnerable, the priority of moral formation, and a posture of discernment toward a technology that is grown rather than built, while diverging sharply on the moral status of AI.
